items.title: Barbie Rewind Review
items.author: Rachel Weber
items.content:
Barbie Rewind feels like the equivalent of showing your children the family heirloom rocking horse, and then watching them poke it and ask if they can play Roblox. A weird mix of nostalgia and interior decorating sim, it's home to 17 retro Barbie games and a dreamhouse to arrange Barbie-appropriate furniture in. Now, it's been over three decades since I last smashed a Barbie against a G.I. Joe and made smooching noises, so I called in two gaming experts, Kora (9) and Paloma (5), to assist with this review. Sadly, unlike her looks, time has not been kind to Barbie's gaming legacy.

Why does she have a scuba mask but not a toilet?

"That doesn't make sense. Why does she have a scuba mask but not a toilet?" A crucial question from Kora as the girls got stuck into the only bit of Barbie Rewind they actually cared about: the decorating. This might be selling itself as a collection of Barbie games from 1991's NES Barbie through to 2007's Barbie as the Island Princess, but its newly created Dreamhouse mode is the big winner here. There are more than 250 pieces of furniture, and some of them are unlocked by playing the retro Barbie games. The big B and other characters like Ken and Christie give you quests, but they're just to decorate the house, so it's a bit like someone saying "be careful" when you're already falling down the stairs.

The Barbie games themselves got what I would call a polite fiddle. I played all of them before the expert advisors were called in, and Rewind is heavy on minigames of the platforming and "catch the falling coconut" variety. These games haven't been given the Monkey Island-style reboot; they're presented seemingly entirely as is, but with a frame that relates to their various consoles to help smooth over any aspect ratio issues.

It's great as a museum piece, but show it to anyone born after 2010 and they basically look like cave paintings. "Is that meant to be Barbie?" asks Kora incredulously, squinting at Barbie Pet Rescue. Paloma picks up the controller to play one of the minigames, a sort of cat Pong using two paws that is apparently essential to pet care, and watches the ball of yarn awkwardly bounce off the screen. She knows controllers, she plays Lego Batman, but this minigame makes no sense. The ball is slow, the angles are off, and Paloma looks at me exasperated as if I personally offended her.

Controls were an issue throughout, changing between games in a way that meant looking up the button layout for everything they wanted to try. One smart addition is the option to tweak things like your total health in certain games, which makes for a less stressful experience all round. The girls liked the concept of a lot of them – veterinarian duties, horse racing, and the fashion dress-up doll in particular – but these are kids born long after the time when you knew that what you saw on the cover of a game was light years away from how it actually looked. I could burn through pixelated bouncing and stilted dialogue on nostalgia alone, but Kora and Paloma are playing Hogwarts Legacy; they have iPad games, and their eyes know not the trauma of staring into a Gameboy Color in the back of a moving vehicle.

items.title: 12 12 12 Review
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This is a spoiler-free review of the first two episodes of , streaming on Apple TV now.

Apple TV’s 12 12 12 operates under these invented cardinal rules of a professional heist: It takes 12 months to plan, 12 hours to execute, and if the cops don’t catch the perpetrators in 12 days, they never will. (Why this didn’t premiere on December 12, I’ll never understand.) The series rests its entire weight on this premise, hopping between the three phases of a heist organized by Jamie Dornan’s Paul Galvin, a retired thief pulled back in for one last job, and the FBI agent relentlessly on his trail, Anthony Mackie’s Jack Strickland. The question is, then, does 12 12 12’s gimmick work? Based on the first two episodes, “I’m robbing the house on Christmas Eve while the family’s at mass” and “I Want My Halo Back,” the answer seems to be: not really.

12 12 12 starts with eyebrow-raising intrigue, as a crumpled, naked man slithers out of a lockbox inside a fancy-looking bank vault and starts cracking open safes. But the cutaway from this scene — right into the 12 12 12 explanation — is only the first instance of the main problem with the show thus far: switching over to a new window of time kills any of the momentum the previous scenes had going for them. 12 12 12 also approaches each of its nonlinear storylines with the same level of urgency. Hour 1 of Paul’s heist to steal the equivalent of one billion physical U.S. dollars — which, just how bulky is that in comparison, say, to the Breaking Bad storage unit stack? — from a Swiss bank moves with practically the same verve as Jack getting wise to what’s happened on the Day 1 hunt. It doesn’t help with differentiating either when both characters keep referencing “what happened in Newark” as the murky botched job from the past they won’t shut the hell up about nor actually explain beyond the obvious trauma they incurred from it.

12 12 12’s first two episodes, written by Dudi Appleton and Jim Keebble, treat that concept as though it’s that the audience could only follow the plot by spoon-feeding us time and place, and the script doubles down on this. The plot itself is full of cliches so that when it posits an occasionally unique idea it, by comparison, feels nearly revelatory. Of course, it often squanders that goodwill just as quickly. Just when you think 12 12 12 is going somewhere, its timeline triptych appears and swipes over to a new time period, resetting the action and deflating any of the excitement the show had just built. The dialogue is full of insufferable back-and-forths that are either inane or could have come from nearly any primetime cable procedural that’s attempting a quippy Marvel-ized punch-up.

Mackie and Dornan, two very competent actors, both make great efforts to do what they can with the trite material but to little avail. There’s only so much even accomplished actors can do with lines like “What if the only thing I’m good at is being a thief?” as Paul contemplates his girlfriend’s surprise pregnancy, or “You stole from me, Galvin. Now you’re gonna know how it feels,” as Jack promises to get revenge on Paul. For a show about pulling off the biggest bank heist in European history, it’s botched the job.

items.title: Heartland Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Heartland is streaming on Netflix now.

A former country rock star searches for her missing niece in Shana Feste’s Heartland, a film with the broad appearance of a neo-noir, but one that doesn’t have nearly enough thrills or intrigue. The story comes from a place of love, both for country music and for Nashville. However, it unfolds too mechanically to unearth the seedy underbelly at which it hints, making for lackluster mystery despite Jessica Chastain’s enormous efforts at drawing emotions from a tepid script.

It begins interestingly enough, with Chastain’s washed-up, tough-as-nails musician Misty Jones huddled over a grave as she tearfully buries her dog before threatening the neighbor who killed it. None of this has any bearing on the larger plot, but it paints Misty as a cornered animal; she has nothing and no one. Her fridge is scant except for a forgotten Grammy she stores there for safe-keeping, a fun bit of environmental storytelling by way of visual information. Before long, though, this becomes the movie’s default lingua franca, with an unending number of shots of photographs and documents to try and piece together a whodunnit when Misty’s niece — the daughter of her estranged brother, an up-and-coming country artist named Charlie Heart (Carter Faith) — turns up missing.

This draws Misty back to the Nashville music scene, where she navigates ineffectual cops and seedy industry figures while retracing Charlie’s steps. The mystery of her disappearance runs parallel to Misty reacquainting herself with her problem-child past and through predatory people and places she once knew, leading to an eventual overlap of these simultaneous threads by way of a family secret. However, each time Heartland features a major reveal, it zips forward far too quickly alongside its umpteenth country music cue, as though it were entering some well-established final act.

In the process, what you’re left with is a story where Misty stumbles her way into information or ping-pongs between various characters — like Garett Hedlund’s charismatic producer Roy Combs — and ends up feeling like an inactive protagonist despite technically driving the plot. She moves from place to place, but rare are the moments when she puts two and two together. Chastain is remarkably locked-in as the aging country star — a woman who doesn’t want to be seen but is forced back into the spotlight. However, as convincing as her conception of Misty may be, it doesn’t matter all that much when every plot turn seems to fall into her lap.

This passive experience is further marred by mechanical filmmaking. While it all technically coheres — the nighttime spaces, lit by halogen signs, are all appropriately noxious; Feste manages to capture Chastain’s close-ups with clarity — you could practically set your watch by how each subplot plays out, and the way learning something new sends Misty charging to a new location at the end of practically every scene. It’s a languid film with no breathing room, an oxymoron that makes sense once the film winds up and you can recount how much has happened by way of plot, and how little by way of story or emotional development. For instance, there are hints and flashbacks about her ex-husband and musical partner Clark (John Hawkes) throughout, but his appearance is relegated to late in the runtime while his actual role as a specter of her past ends up with little actual impact.

Its country music interludes play like wheel-spinning interruptions despite gesturing at phantom connections between violence and the genre at large.

The pieces for some other more rigorous story all appear to be in place, from people Misty knows she can’t trust to former friends with whom she needs to make amends. Unfortunately, Heartland strings these together in rote fashion. Its camera is used to tell more than to show, and its country music interludes play like wheel-spinning interruptions despite gesturing at phantom connections between violence and the genre at large. The film, as a whole, feels episodic and disconnected.

Through it all, Chastain remains remarkable as ever; unfortunately, it’s as a woman who would rather be anywhere else — a feeling that’s hard to shake when sitting down to watch Heartland for yourself.

items.title: Yaga Episode 5 Recap and Review
items.author: Jessie Wade
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Season 1, Episode 5. Episodes 1-5 are now streaming on AMC+ in the US and Crave in Canada, with new episodes releasing on Fridays at midnight PT.

Following up on Episode 4’s chaotic and eventful ending, Episode 5 gives us the most reveals we’ve seen yet in Yaga. Picking up right where we left, we find out Laney is not in fact dead, but instead went into cardiac arrest – with a pissed off Eckert yelling at both Carson and Rapp for being the cause of it.

Rapp explains his theory as to what is happening in this town, which includes Laney thinking she is Baba Yaga and luring people such as Henry, Logan, Angel, and others into her chicken hut in the woods for manifestation rituals and sacrifices.

As they go their separate ways, we find out more unhinged details involving this mystery. Rapp ends up seeing a little girl (who very well may be a vision) who echoes what Laney said in the hospital – that Henry is a “bad dog” and is in Baba Yaga’s chicken house. Immediately after, Rapp finds a mysterious package in his rental car, and upon opening it, he finds a carved box with chicken feathers and what looks to be Henry’s phone. The sinister mask is set as the phone’s background and there’s a raw audio recording for him to play of the podcast episode Henry did with Katherine, which unfolds into fascinating revelations.

On the other side of things, Carson and Eckert are trying to track down who uploaded the video of Logan’s body by speaking to various people around town. One of the familiar faces is Katherine, who throughout the episode (and the show overall) seems to constantly drop suspicious clues, almost too casually, for it to not be intentional.

From mentioning the diner owner, Geena, cooking the chickens who stop laying eggs, to telling Carson she and Rapp “look good together” while giving her a sly look, to bumping into Eckert and seeing images of the mask, telling him she loves the artist’s work, Katherine seems to be dropping information right into their laps. And in this episode, it’s more apparent than it’s ever been.

As Rapp continues on his search in the woods, we see Katherine in her office with Henry recording the podcast, and surprisingly, Logan is there to manage the tech of it all. This is the first time we get to really see Hudson Williams at length as Henry, and his portrayal of the billionaire playboy is chilling while he tries to charm Katherine with his outright crude methods.

It’s pretty apparent that Henry is trying to get information on Baba Yaga for some reason, as he inquires about witches eating bones and casually mentions the retreat he attends – all with an obvious underlying sexual interest in Katherine.

Carrie-Anne Moss as Katherine absolutely owns this episode with her incredible storytelling and her ability to bewitch anyone in her orbit. By the end of the podcast (and the episode as a whole) you’re left wondering who actually seduced who into their bed? Who holds the power of the seduction?

The theme of men being inappropriate and downright sexually assaulting women in this show rears its ugly head yet again, with Henry having deliberately brushed his hand against Katherine’s breast without consent, and Eckert kissing Carson while they were at his house working on the case. In the latter scene, she shoves him off of her and he comments, “it’s not like I was trying to fuck you.” It’s a disturbing but accurate reality for many people and the show bringing this theme to light is as important as it is difficult to watch.

“Women? We’re angry about everything.”

As night comes – and right when we think Rapp is actually focusing on being responsible – he makes his way over to Katherine’s house, surprising her. Yet she invites him in for dinner. While they discuss the podcast and details from it that Rapp is trying to get answers on, Katherine continues her casual attitude and shares how she relates to Baba Yaga. “She resonates with me, with women. She’s a figure of great power, wisdom, rage.” Rapp asks her if she’s angry about something, to which Katherine responds, “Women? We’re angry about everything.” Any woman watching this scene will likely relate to the safe door Moss just opened with the perfection that is that line.

Towards the end of the episode, we can sense how intoxicating the sexual tension is that has built up between Katherine and Rapp as, filled with passion and lust, they grab each other to have sex on her living room floor. On the opposite side of things, we get confirmation of Carson’s feelings for Rapp as she’s at her place, rightfully upset over her assault and that Rapp wouldn’t respond to her texts, as we see her sniff his tank top in her hands while pleasuring herself in the same moments Rapp and Katherine are having sex.

After they finish, we see Rapp looking at his reflection in the bathroom mirror – taking in the nail and bite marks and other bruises – when a vision seems to flicker through. Henry’s standing next to him, puts his hand around his throat and pulls him in for a brutal kiss. All of a sudden, Henry looks into the mirror, opens his mouth, and screams as blood pours out of it.

In that moment, the scene stops and jumps to Rapp jolting and standing in the hallway as he hears someone scream and pound on Katherine’s front door. He looks toward the clock on the wall, seeing the time flip to 3:33, and then sees Geena’s daughter, Lily, at the door. She starts throwing up blood as Katherine runs to grab her, while Rapp finds a tooth on the ground and holds it up in curiosity.

We’re now left with more questions than we started in this episode, including finding out Henry bought three of the creepy witch masks from the artist, while Rapp discovered a large triskele symbol made out of moss in the middle of the woods – which seems to be the circle Laney uses for her retreats. We also find out Katherine gifted Henry the Aztec knife that was allegedly the murder weapon for Logan, while lying smoothly to Rapp about it. Who do we think is behind all of this? Is there one true Baba Yaga or is it a cult of culprits?

items.title: Ebenezer Review
items.author: Tom Jorgensen
items.content:
One need only look to The Muppet Christmas Carol, the best Christmas movie of them all, to understand why Charles Dickens’ novella has endured countless adaptations over the nearly two hundred years since it was published. The miserly Ebenezer Scrooge’s confrontation with the ghosts of his past with hopes for a brighter future is so fundamentally strong that a staging of it by Michael Caine and Kermit the Frog that blends all sorts of tones and meta commentary has room not only to work, but to stand as an unambiguously respected adaptation of the text. Ti West’s Ebenezer feels most focused on illuminating the darker corners of Dickens’ tale, but the broad and classically Johnny Depp performance at its heart holds it back from ever elevating into a more meaningful adaptation of the text.

A Christmas Carol is, of course, a ghost story at its heart, and Ti West’s long history in the horror genre - including a ghost story of his own, The Innkeepers - makes him an interesting director to see paired with the material. West’s instincts on how and where to amp up A Christmas Carol’s spooky trappings are strong from the top down, and they’re most evident in Ebenezer’s production design. Ebenezer leans on the austere chill of its Victorian London setting well with practical sets and stages that instantly read as Christmas Carol-appropriate. The destitute and dour look of the film illuminates both the poverty Scrooge hates and the corresponding spiritual bankruptcy from which he suffers in equal measure. Tyler Bates’ string-heavy score helps to push that sense of unease, with the highlight piece being a driving and ominous string quartet version of “Carol of the Bells” played over the opening credits of Londoners bringing out decorations and getting ready for the approaching holiday.

While Ebenezer is largely a faithful adaptation of Dickens’ novella, West and writer Nathaniel Halpern embellish certain turns of the plot to underscore either Scrooge’s inner turmoil or the story’s horror elements, like adding a new prologue featuring Scrooge’s business partner Jacob Marley (Ian McKellen). The prologue serves the dual purpose of starting West’s darker take on the story off with a body (“Marley wasdead: to begin with,” and all that) and giving McKellen just a little bit more time on camera. Formative events like Ebenezer’s tough childhood or his failed engagement with Belle get expounded on with enough care to work on their own merits, but with Depp’s Ebenezer tough to connect to emotionally, little of the new additions wind up feeling impactful enough to justify the time spent on them. Despite coming in just under two hours, each of the “staves” that Ebenezer is chaptered into routinely taper off in momentum before West is moving on to the next act of the story.

A director’s influence can only take Ebenezer Scrooge’s story so far. Any staging of A Christmas Carol lives and dies on the casting of its Scrooge: the whole story is told over Scrooge’s shoulder, and whatever catharsis the audience is able to experience through Scrooge’s own as he wakes up on Christmas Day a changed man has to be channeled through an accessible and readably human performance. That leaves Johnny Depp’s work here as Ebenezer Scrooge feeling like a frustrating misfire.

Depp’s conception of Scrooge, with all of its physical business and explosive emotion, feels better suited to stage than screen.

Depp’s Scrooge is a constant source of lively and unpredictable energy through the well-trodden events of Ebenezer’s story, it’s just not at all clear by the end of the film that it was the right energy for the more straightforward approach West employs throughout the rest of the film. Depp’s conception of Scrooge, with all of its physical business and explosive emotion, feels better suited to stage than screen. What’s all the more frustrating is that Depp is not only capable of stepping down the zaniness of his Scrooge when called on, but he’s far better in the role when doing so. The few moments throughout the film where Depp plays Scrooge with some reserve, like when trying to break through to his past selves to beg them to do things differently, connect pretty effectively, and the final stretch where Scrooge is able to rejoice in his overnight rebirth gives Depp’s manic approach to the character a better fitting context.

With Depp’s campy performance pushing Ebenezer’s otherwise macabre presentation to its breaking point, supporting players like Rupert Grint, Ellie Bamber, and Sam Claflin do a lot to keep the story grounded in more recognizable feelings. Grint’s affability as Scrooge’s clerk Bob Cratchit cuts Depp’s hissing negativity well, and Ebenezer could have used more of the genuine light that he and the Cracthit family contributes, if only for the contrast to make all of the film’s darkness feel that much more oppressive.

On that note, points to whoever was responsible for casting Freddie Lee-Grey as Tiny Tim: he has nary more to say than “god bless us, everyone”, but wow, does that kid step up to the plate and knock it out of the park when called to do so. As Scrooge’s nephew Fred, Claflin embodies the optimism and good nature that Scrooge detests with ease, with Daisy Ridley stopping by for what amounts to a cameo as Fred’s more skeptical wife Clara and walking away with one of the film’s bigger laughs. Bamber’s Belle is just as effective as Fred at portraying the warmth that Scrooge willingly and cruelly let go of years before.

West makes no attempt to give the spirits that visit Ebenezer any cheery or pleasant characteristics: they’re dead and they hate it, and from the looks of them, they have good reason to feel that way. McKellen’s Marley does get a brief moment to act as a canary in a moral coalmine for Scrooge early on, but he’s mostly here to lend some gravitas to the obligatory “you will be haunted by three spirits” moment, the kind of thing he’s been doing in his sleep for decades. Not helping his efforts at all are the cheap-looking visual effects doing the work to create McKellen’s spectral form. The poor quality of the visual effects extends to the dozens of nameless ghosts that arrive to put the fear of Father Christmas in Scrooge’s heart by banging on windows and going “ooh” and “ahh”, plaguing both he and the audience throughout the film.

Thankfully, the headliner Ghosts of Christmases Past, Present, and Yet to Come are better designed and realized. Andrea Riseborough’s bride-like Ghost of Christmas Past is the most outwardly eerie, with milky eyes and a detached, childlike voice which really cut through Depp’s bombast as Scrooge revisits a painful chapter of his younger days. Riseborough’s performance is monotone by design, but West supports Risebrough’s ethereal presence with some of the film’s more outwardly horror-coded cinematography, with some effective long takes that pull a sort of “Texas switch” by having her teleport quickly and creepily across long distances. Tramell Tillman’s Ghost of Christmas Present is more mercurial, and Tillman’s intensity and lack of patience with Scrooge’s waffling both give the sense that he could throttle Scrooge at the drop of a nightcap. The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come maintains the slow-moving, wordless and faceless presentation it usually does, but West at least gives it a haunting Predator-like clicking sound to set it apart.

items.title: Paper Tiger Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
With Paper Tiger, director James Gray returns to a milieu familiar from his first three movies – Little Odessa, The Yards, and – and delivers one of his strongest films in years.

At the heart of this slow burn crime drama – set in Queens, New York in 1986 – are two brothers, family man Irwin Pearl (Miles Teller) and his older brother Gary (Adam Driver), a swaggering former cop who comes to his younger sibling with a business proposition. Utilizing his ties to City Hall, Gary wants to launch a consulting firm offering their services to recently arrived Russian immigrants who have started a clean-up firm for the polluted Gowanus Canal.

Gary, the wheeler-dealer, would get the Russians hooked up with his connections while straight-shooter Irwin, an engineer, would advise them on how to keep the operation up to code. With Gary being bled dry in a divorce and Irwin considering his eldest son’s looming college tuition, this business venture seems like a win-win for both brothers. Unfortunately, these Russians are actually a mob front. When Irwin sees them doing something he shouldn’t have witnessed, he, his wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) and their two teenage boys are targeted.

Irwin and his family are not street-smart people. They’re a painfully ordinary, working-class family where the most dangerous thing they’ve seen is the revolver that ex-cop Gary keeps holstered to his ankle. Gary is essentially the serpent who enters their modest paradise, tempting Irwin to desire more than he already possesses. (The movie begins with a quote from Aeschylus: "Let there be wealth without tears; enough for the wise man who will ask no further.")

Gary is slick and has big ambitions, but he’s not a bad guy. As shady as he seems, it’s surprising to discover that, even when he was a cop, Gary possessed a moral compass. Adam Driver is, unsurprisingly, great here, revealing the complexities of a man who, like the titular paper tiger, may not be all that he blusters he is. Gary, who only allows his real vulnerabilities to be seen when alone, clearly loves his brother and extended family – even though he’s ultimately responsible for the danger they’re in. What he’s prepared to do about that puts him to the test.

Irwin is essentially impotent to protect his family, relying on Gary’s aid, who in turn thinks being a former cop will protect him. The Russians, though, aren’t La Cosa Nostra and Gary can’t cajole, bluff or bargain with these criminals the way he might have with the Gambinos once upon a time.

Ditching the bravado that marked his earlier roles, Miles Teller is a revelation as Irwin, a weak man trying to muster guts in a situation where he’s woefully out of his depth. He’s a schlub who makes dad jokes, not a guy who knows the ways of the street. Irwin here reminds me of Dustin Hoffman’s characters in Straw Dogs and Marathon Man, while Driver’s richly nuanced, “ain’t I a big man” performance is reminiscent of Gene Hackman or Robert Duvall’s work in their prime.

Meanwhile, Scarlett Johansson gives one of her best performances as Hester, a New York housewife with big curly hair who runs a tight household – and is keeping a big secret from her husband and beloved sons. Johansson’s reaction in a scene where Hester learns some shocking news is utterly authentic and heartbreaking.

The fear that upends the Pearl family’s life is so palpable because it’s utterly alien to their bland, ordinary world. They’re ill-equipped for the peril they’re in, as highlighted by an incredibly creepy home invasion sequence where what you hear is more unnerving than what you can see.

Shot on 35mm film by cinematographer Joaquin Baca-Asay, Paper Tiger looks like it really was made in the 1970s or ‘80s, with its graininess and imperfections adding to its period authenticity. Likewise, production designer Happy Massee and costume designer Amy Roth succeed in making Paper Tiger feel lived-in and genuine. You can practically smell the ash trays and Brut cologne.

items.title: South Park Season 29, Episode 5 Review: 'We Be Clubbin''
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
I think we can officially give up on the notion of South Park Season 29 having any real sort of overarching narrative. Episode 5 comes and goes without even a nod to the recurring "GTA 6 is coming" gag, much less an attempt to build on the previous episodes in a significant way. The series has clearly swung back around to emphasizing standalone stories and trying to dig deeper into its ensemble cast. On paper, that's hardly the worst idea in the world, but for the third episode in a row, the execution leaves something to be desired.

I actually had pretty high hopes for "We Be Clubbin'." The Tweek/Craig relationship is one of the more low-key charming subplots in the series, and these two are long overdue for some time in the spotlight. This episode acknowledges as much when Cartman realizes to his horror that he and his classmates forgot the duo's anniversary. But for as much potential as a Heated Rivalry parody with Tweek and Craig in the lead roles had, this episode doesn't do enough to capitalize on that potential.

Once again, you have an episode that's guilty of beating the same horse over and over again till it's well past dead. This time the topic du jour is club sports and the predatory way they consume families' time, money, and sanity. In that sense, Tweek and his already anxiety-ridden family are perfect vessels through which to attack the institution. The problem, as is too often the case with South Park, is that the same jokes get repeated over and over again. We can only spend so long watching Tweek's parents wake up at 5am, rush around the state, whip out the old credit card, and deal with the other overachieving parents before the humor is just gone.

I mainly wish this episode had actually focused on Tweek and Craig more. What we do get from "We Be Clubbin'" in terms of relationship drama is pretty satisfying, but there's just not enough of that element. I would have liked the episode to fully commit to spoofing Heated Rivalry and get into the actual sports more (though I suppose that's the whole joke — there are no sports in club sports). It might also have helped if we saw more of Cartman and the gang sprinkled throughout the episode. But after the opening couple of scenes, those characters all but disappear from the episode.

Coming into Episode 5, I was also intensely curious to see how the show would reference the recent midterm elections. There's been a strong sense all season long that the writers really aren't that interested in focusing on topical political humor this season, and that's basically confirmed in the opening scene where Mr. Garrison reminds us it's no fun to punch down on "a fat loser." That scene is pretty entertaining in its brief acknowledgement of recent events, particularly as PC Principal drops the Power Christian shtick and returns to his old ways. I was also amused by the attempt to circle back around to the midterms at the end with Tweek's line, "You got swindled by a fat con man who played into your anxieties."

Episode 5 at least its head in the right place. It focuses on current events opnly as much as is strictly necessary before pivoting to a more standalone story geared around two underutilized characters. It just doesn't make the most of its premise or ultimately focus on said characters enough. And so Season 29's rough patch continues. Can the long-awaited arrival of GTA finally turn things around in the season finale? Let's hope so.

items.title: Being Heumann Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
is in theaters now and debuts November 13 on Apple TV.

Disability activist Judith Heumann has the perfect name for a story about forcing politicians to acknowledge the humanity of an underclass. More perfect still is the title of her memoir, Being Heumann, which CODA director Sian Heder turns into a straightforward but occasionally rousing biopic revolving around a political sit-in, a film whose authentic casting is a vital part of its form.

Beginning with a failed streetside protest in 1972, the movie zips forward several years into the work of a bustling coalition with busy offices. The year is 1977, and the wheelchair-using Heumann, aka Judy (Ruth Madeley, a wheelchair-user herself), is among a group of several protesters furious with the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare’s (HEW) preening secretary Joseph Califano Jr. (Mark Ruffalo) for refusing to sign a vital equality act into law. Some in Judy’s camp are blind or Deaf; others are para- or quadriplegic; and a small handful are able-bodied allies from queer or racial advocacy groups like the Black Panthers. As they gather outside the HEW offices in San Francisco, Judy makes impromptu demands for a building occupation until Califano Jr. signs the aforementioned legislation, referred to as “Section 504.”

There is, however, a moral wrinkle to Judy's plan. Her cohorts soon discover that she packed a toothbrush; it was always her plan to enter the building and stay overnight. That the fierce equality advocate refused to share this with her protesters makes her self-absorbed in a particularly compelling way, as her eyes are gradually opened to the ways in which her actions do or do not gel with her fellow protesters. Among them is the fellow polio-stricken Ed Roberts (Michael Patrick Thornton), who can’t join this leveling-up of Judy’s praxis because he needs to sleep in an iron lung. Roberts’ role is therefore minor, but the frankness with which Thornton performs it makes him an absolute must-watch.

This is true for practically the entire cast, beginning with Judy herself, who Madeley imbues with a fearsome, acerbic, and headstrong attitude that slowly reveals deep insecurities as her fellow advocates — including soft-spoken organization newcomer Kitty Cone (Madeline Delp) — push back on her methods during the occupation, yielding entertaining skirmishes. The movie’s tone, therefore, veers between challenging, comedic, and broadly uplifting, as its focus falls on numerous in-group debates and conversations while the activist contingent waits for the targets of their protests to respond.

While the film occasionally leans towards prescriptive and verbose — its scenes often pivot around characters having to explain their views in detail — this is part and parcel of Heder’s particular telling, which aims to bring crisscrossing political debates about disability activism to the fore. Being Heumann is at its most interesting when its many heroic subjects disagree, a prickliness which eventually leads to a greater cooperation down the line.

The real sit-in lasted nearly four weeks, and Heder details every challenge along the way as able-bodied allies like Dylan O’Brien’s news reporter, Evan White, and Ray Fisher’s Panther member, Chuck Jackson, embed themselves with the group to assist and observe while supportive politicians like Congressman George Miller (Rob Delaney) assist from the outside. This, too, ends up a meta-textual piece of the movie’s telling; these relatively well-known actors are the kind that get smaller-budgeted movies green-lit, and that they cede space to the central cast feels in and of itself like an act of allyship.

The ensemble is made up of relative unknowns, and that their own disabilities are in line with those of their characters serves a dual purpose. The first is verisimilitude: Freed from the constraints of having to concentrate on “performing” disability, they each bring a remarkable and personable realism to their roles, including Andrew Pilkington as Hale Zukas, a nonverbal activist with cerebral palsy who communicates with a helmet-mounted pointer and a board full of letters. That he spells out each word slowly is no hurdle to the character’s sharp, sarcastic wit (“Disability is not a tragedy,” he spells, as a fellow protester interprets for the larger group. “It is a tremendous hassle.”). Similarly, when we catch glimpses of Judy’s morning routine, involving being helped to the bathroom by an attendant who shows up rather late, her understandably rankled attitude takes center stage, both fleshing her out as a character while fueling her advocacy in the first place.

The second and equally important purpose of casting disabled actors is as an act of equity. Section 504 may be about ramps for wheelchair-users, readers for the blind, interpreters for the Deaf, and so on — a costly endeavor according to Califano Jr. — but its real goal is equal access to jobs and education. Nearly every character on screen occupies the HEW building because they’ve been denied opportunities owing to their disabilities (Judy, for instance, was denied her teaching license). So, granting these roles to disabled actors, which they might ordinarily lose to able-bodied peers who have had more chances to bolster their résumés, is the movie putting its money where its mouth is. Califano Jr. complains about being asked to remake the world, but the production does it with ease.

Granting these roles to disabled actors, which they might ordinarily lose to able-bodied peers who have had more chances to bolster their résumés, is the movie putting its money where its mouth is. 

Since the film is a large ensemble piece, Heder makes minor alterations to traditional framing; her eye-level medium and group shots are much closer to the ground to accommodate the wheelchair-using cast, and the frame expands laterally to capture them. These are only minor adjustments, but they speak to the fluidity of Heder’s filmmaking, wherein she tells broad and familiar stories by changing their packaging ever-so-slightly. Similarly, her Best Picture winner, CODA, not only casts real Deaf adults in major roles, but the movie’s editing follows the rhythm of their signed dialogue rather than the traditional beats of spoken words. And, much like CODA, Being Heumann doesn’t shy away from the full dimensions of is disabled subjects, including their sex lives; in the process, it makes the sit-in seem pretty fun and hedonistic.

Heder’s minor departures help contort the screen to include a wider array of people within the bounds of a traditionally mawkish but no less effective political biopic. Granted, a handful of beats remain too obvious and on-the-nose to really work — like the out-of-place use of the Ramones’ “Judy is a Punk” accompanied by slow-motion wheelchair-rolling — but the movie is ultimately a crowd-pleasing delight, which is the sort of thing Heder excels at making.

items.title: Tanuki: Pon's Summer Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
Frost hasn't yet replaced New England's morning dew, but cold air is starting to settle in. Days feel short, and the sun sets before I've signed off from work for the day. I complain all summer about the heat, then want it back just as it starts to fade: Long, meandering days that are full of potential. It feels fitting – and maybe a bit ironic – that as soon as my mind (and maybe yours) starts wandering back to summer, Kyoto-based studio Denkiworks released its homage to summer in rural Japan with Tanuki: Pon's Summer. It's a game that feels just as warm as the summer depicted, and a nice reprieve from the looming cold.

Tanuki: Pon's Summer is set in an idyllic Japanese countryside that's centered around an aging shrine. Pon, the tanuki tasked with tending to it, let the shrine's grounds crumble while he ate chips and played video games. Tanuki gods bully Pon into getting his act together and fixing the shrine before a big festival. But that'll cost money, and money comes from a job. Pon's skills are limited, but he does have a BMX bike. To the post office it is! You play through a month of Pon's summer, delivering the island's mail to earn money to fix the shrine, and days are all marked on a calendar. Along the way, it so perfectly captures the lazy opportunity of summer in its moment-to-moment about a relaxed town.

The island is not big, but it's quite dense with several distinct, lively parts of town and Pon must figure out how to get around efficiently on his bike. (You can walk; Pon can't jump on foot, but can on his bike, so walking for even short distances is not effective.) Conveniently, the island is bike-friendly, especially BMX bike-friendly with the makings of a skatepark. So, delivering mail is not just a thing you do – it's the draw.

Each day, Pon picks up the mail from the post office, stacking them in a basket through a Tetris-like minigame that feels like a welcome ritual each in-game day. Then, he heads out. Tanuki: Pon's Summer is open-world in the sense that you can make deliveries in any order, but the storyline is linear. Some of the packages are simple dropoffs, but others have an activity or a storyline attached to them and to the people of the island. Among them are rival sushi and yakitori chefs, a creatively-stifled photographer, and a tough guy with a soft spot. All of these characters are delightfully weird, and their stories follow suit.

Those rival chefs, for instance, have some longstanding beef between each other, and aren't initially very nice to Pon, either. They know him as a lazy tanuki who let the shrine crumble, and throughout Pon's month as a mailman, their attitudes toward each other (and Pon!) soften. Pon's adventure, too, helps reunite an estranged father and daughter, who are both artisan makers. Tanuki: Pon's Summer may have Pon in the name, but it's hardly Pon's story that's being told. It's a charming one that's more focused on the relationships between people on the island and the community they make together.

Crucially, each of these island residents needs help with something, which is where Tanuki: Pon's Summer's minigames come in. And there are a lot, like skewering meat and veggies to make yakitori, stacking pieces of sushi to order, sanding logs, serving shaved ice and foamy beer, checking out customers at the convenience store, playing the drums for a local musician, hitting home runs at the local baseball field. Minigames like these (and a bunch others) mimic that sort of delight of childhood summers in which anything seemed possible. They're the sorts of small adventures that break up drifting days in the summer heat.

You could put all sorts of descriptors on it: a mail delivery simulator, a BMX freestyle game, or a cooking game.

But not all of these minigames are as joyous, though. Several of them feel like a monotonous drag where Pon sands down logs at a snail's pace or another that forces Pon to cut down far too many bamboo stalks. Sure, we had to do chores on a summer break, but I resented some of the minigames for taking me away from the excitement of riding Pon's bike around town and many of the other things I'd have rather been doing.

You could put all sorts of descriptors on it, whether that's a mail delivery simulator, a BMX freestyle game, or a cooking game. And oftentimes, this approach brought a lot of whimsy and a steady variety from moment to moment. But there were a bit too many where I wanted Tanuki: Pon's Summer to let me get back to the thing I liked most about the game: Riding around on Pon's bike.

The core of Tanuki: Pon's Summer is getting from place to place on his bike while making an extreme sport out of it. He bunny hops over small cliffs, grinds down handrails, and pulls off tricks over gaps and soars over sunny rooftops. Tricks are simple enough to pull off by directional stick movements and button inputs while in air, but stringing them together for combos is a bit more tricky. Optional challenges dotted around the island offer a chance to test your skill, but otherwise the game doesn't ask Pon to prove himself, aside from the occasional request where a resident asks Pon to do some tricks, under a time limit, to reach a certain number of points. (All tricks amass points, which typically don't mean anything. It pops up on screen even if you're doing a barspin into a wheelie on your way to just deliver a model kit.) It doesn't necessarily need to ask, because the BMX freestyle itself is a blast. On deliveries, I longed for long stretches of road to see how far I could make Pon wheelie. I used helpfully placed ramps to look for new routes and bounced from roof top to roof top just to show off.

The worst of Tanuki: Pon's Summer's minigames either lingered for too long or felt dull compared to the fun of his bike. Although they are relatively short, those select minigames (emphasis on mini) dragged in a way that broke up the momentum I'd have from riding around town and doing tricks on my way to the next delivery. Most of them don't repeat – Pon is asked once, for instance, to balance and roll boulders through a tricky maze or to pour the perfect beers from a bar's tap. Once Pon's done, he's done. He's moved on to the next task, and whoever asked for his help won't ask him to do that particular chore again, but they may ask for some other sort of help.

The worst of Tanuki: Pon's Summer's minigames either lingered for too long or felt dull compared to the fun of his bike.

The last piece of Tanuki: Pon's Summer to talk about is the shrine decor, which is entirely optional. People who enjoyed decorating their Animal Crossing: New Horizons islands may be drawn to this in particular. Slowly, more of the shrine opens up big, empty swaths of land you can decorate – up to you whether or not it's worthwhile. Pon collects decor and furniture from the quests he's set upon by islanders, but he can also purchase stuff from the kitsune lingering around. His overarching goal is about getting the shrine together for the big festival, but the decorating simulator felt extraneous for me. There's no real parameters here to guide the direction or to make the feature feel consequential in any way – it's just something to do. Again, it felt like a slower piece of the game that took me away from the parts I liked best.

Playing through Tanuki: Pon's Summer took about 10 hours. Most of this time was following the storyline, doing challenges, and messing around on the bike, but some of this time was redoing days lost from game-breaking pre-release bugs. The autosave feature is not so generous, and it'd be smart to make frequent use of the manual save feature in case bugs persist past the launch window.

items.title: How to Rob a Bank Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Clearly, we live in notably crappy times in numerous ways, and clearly, there’s a lot to be fed up with about how the system seems so egregiously stacked against most of us while the rich constantly get richer. So sure, it’s good to have a big studio movie at least to tackle these issues, but How to Rob a Bank never actually has enough to say about the topic except for reinforcing that yeah, this sucks, but hey, at least you can make some fun videos about it.

Nicholas Hoult stars as Ryan, the leader of a group of masked bank robbers who release elaborate videos of their crimes on the internet and have become online sensations as a result. Also filming rehearsed monologues to camera and tutorials on how to emulate their actions — titled, you guessed it, How to Rob a Bank — Ryan and his crew, which includes Emi (Anna Sawai), Vince (Pete Davidson), and Hugo (Rhenzy Feliz), make it clear in their videos that this is all about sticking it to ‘The Man’ and striking back against a world that’s made it so hard to get a financial foothold.

I have no doubt that people posting videos of themselves successfully carrying out a string of bank robberies would go viral, and yet How to Rob a Bank feels wonky from the start because of how overproduced and outright annoying these videos are. They’re filled with animation overlays, loud sound effects, and blaring music in what feels more like Hollywood filmmakers trying to evoke youthful, attention-getting videos rather than coming off as genuine. It doesn’t help that director David Leitch (Deadpool 2, The Fall Guy) sometimes also has this crew do impressive parkour-style flips in the midst of their heists and then gives zero explanation of how this would even be something in their skill set.

John C. Reilly plays FBI Agent West, the guy trying to bring in Ryan’s crew. He ends up recruiting the services of Reagan (Zoë Kravitz), who’s on home arrest after having been convicted of cybercrimes and whose knowledge, West believes, might be useful in tracking down the robbers. Reilly and Kravitz, and the very different energy they bring, actually make for a rather fun unlikely duo, and there are times where I found myself wishing we simply had a mismatched buddy cop-style adventure with them. But ultimately, both of their characters represent how How to Rob a Bank doesn’t follow through on many of the topics it’s bringing up.

Reagan is as anti-establishment as they come, clumsily represented by the stickers on her laptop that look like a checklist of progressive cause catchphrases, while FBI careerman West is very much part of the system. Reagan is also one of the ways the movie name-drops additional troubling and agonizing topics of the moment, from violent cops to school shootings, but even as the two inevitably start to begrudgingly get along, we don’t see either of them actually learn or change all that much in the movie. You might think there could be some drama in Reagan feeling empathy for Ryan’s crew — maybe even trying to help them from the inside — or that they could explore how West feels about being part of a system that can be used for corrupt purposes. But Leitch and writer Mark Bianculli never dig in enough to get more than surface level acknowledgement of anything of the sort.

This goes for the How to Rob a Bank crew as well, who are presented initially as a jovial, fun-loving team and each given a requisite single scene of their home life to try to ground them, with mixed results. Well, that’s except for two other guys in the group beyond the core four, who are so underutilized and often forgotten, it’s bizarre they’re included at all.

It feels a bit, ahem, rich to have a story about financial inequality coming from Jeff Bezos’ Amazon.

Inevitably, the movie takes the turn any story about a group of criminals must take, as the walls begin closing in on our modern day Robin Hoods (who do in fact give much of their stolen money to charity). There are a couple of late reveals about what motivates some of the crew — and how it impacts their past and future — that do carry some emotional weight, but those reveals are held off for too long, and the movie feels paper-thin for too much of its running time. And though they lead into a notably darker portion for a bit, even that feels pushed to the side by the conclusion, as though either the filmmakers or the studio (and yeah, it feels a bit, ahem, rich to have a story about financial inequality coming from Jeff Bezos’ Amazon) were afraid to leave things on too complicated a note.

There are times when you can enjoy the antics of How to Rob a Bank, helped along by its charismatic cast, and there are a couple of moments that shine, including a sequence where we see how the crew deals with being questioned by the cops which features a fun appearance by Young Mazino (Beef, The Last of Us) as their lawyer. We also briefly get moments where actors like Hoult and Sawai remind us that they can be dramatic heavyweights, but too much of the film feels like it’s mistaking loud and frenetic for making an impact as it lightly touches on important topics without actually doing the work to make them resonate.

items.title: The Body Review
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
is streaming on Netflix now. This is a non-spoiler review of the full first season.

The first episode of The Body, titled “Slutty God,” opens with a Bible verse: “Now you are Christ’s body and every one of you is a part of it.” After watching all eight episodes of the new Netflix Catholic high school drama/satire/fever dream, it’s clear that series creator Quinn Shephard did the the extra reading on that passage from First Corinthians 12: “And God has placed in the church first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, of helping, of guidance, and of different kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?”

The Body dabbles in all of the above, literally and metaphorically. Going too deep on it will quickly get into spoiler territory, but The Body mounts a sermon — in the fallout of a high school dance team’s hazing ritual gone wrong — about, well, the body. Is it for pleasure, for purity, for sacrifice? Is it a vessel? What happens when it, both as an individual, or as a parochial community, becomes ill or becomes susceptible to magical thinking? How does one affect the whole?

But let me pull back on the divinity school existentialism here, because while The Body wrestles with all of those things, it is first and foremost a wild and raunchy show about teenagers behaving badly. Set in 2004, the series follows the St. Mark’s dance team — go, Lions! — that initiates their newest member, Grace (Sofia Wylie), at a Halloween party held at an abandoned nunnery nicknamed Devil’s House because, as the myth goes, all the nuns who lived there went crazy. They all take ecstasy and offer Grace as a “prank” sacrifice to the devil so the team can make it to Regionals. But something terrible happens to Grace, setting off an infection of visions and religious hysteria across the team and the town that blurs the line between self-inflicted delirium and unexplainable phenomena. Trying to manage a gaggle of teenage girls and the church’s growing zeal is priest and school principal Father Franklin — whom the girls call Daddy Franklin — played by Nnamdi Asomugha as a stoic nearing his breaking point.

At the center of the mess is Lions’ co-captain Anya (Kristina Bogic, who brings pathos to the cheer captain trope) who, out of necessity, befriends Lisbeth (an excellently freaky Geena Meszaros), a new student who weasels her way onto the team and whose shady past seems to come in handy amid the chaos. Alongside weathering the hysteria and keeping secrets, Anya struggles deeply with her sexuality, refusing to admit her feelings for her best friend and co-captain Elise (Sara Boustany, playing one of the last bastions of sanity throughout the season) is anything more than something that happens when she’s drunk.

The Body is full of sex (and sexual repression) and partying that’s just a sidestep away from Euphoria or Elite, another one of Netflix’s horny high school series. Its litany of influences (or, at least, easy references to explain The Body) are numerous. It’s Yellowjackets (which returns for a final season later this month) if they never crash-landed in the woods. It’s Bring It On if it was overtly queer (so, But I'm a Cheerleader) and R-rated. The Mean Girls, duh. It has shades of the religious fervor found in movies like Carrie, Saint Maud, and The Testament of Ann Lee. Hell, it even has a little sprinkle of Ken Russell’s The Devils’ DNA. (Confess!) Shephard — whose previous work also grapples with the plight of young, often prickly women — channels these touchpoints and shapes them with her own voice into a series that feels immediately relatable yet fresh.

The show’s cast of under-the-radar young actors absolutely works to its benefit — though you might recognize Jackson Kelly, who plays Lisbeth’s brother Leo, as the troubled kid from Season 1 of The Pitt. Without the baggage of being known as “that person from that TV show,” the girls on the dance team, in particular, feel like… well, a Catholic high school girl’s competitive dance team. For as large as the ensemble is, most don’t come off as one-note. Shirley Chen is especially good as Maddie, a Lion who struggles with an eating disorder and intense Catholic guilt. But for a series about a dance team, there’s not nearly enough choreographed dance scenes. When the Lions finally perform at Regionals, it’s hard not to feel robbed of seeing more clever, funny, and beautiful sequences.

The Body is full of the demarcations of 2004: Razrs and Sidekicks, a Kelly Clarkson ringtone and general early aughts soundtrack, bedazzled track suits and bebe shirts, the background of the Bush/Kerry presidential election, and so on. Perennially, the student body mostly has rich parents. The series scratches at teenage conservatism and family wealth — a boy loudly celebrates Bush winning; Anya has an indoor pool and glam squad — but doesn’t go much further. Much like the teenagers themselves, The Body accepts these as , focusing on the intensity of personal feelings. But given that the show has eight one-hour episodes, it could have used a little extra something in the back half as the inner turmoil becomes slightly repetitive.

As the last few episodes begin turning more surreal, The Body goes out on a nebulous ending that is equally frustrating and fascinating. It feels like it’s doing the obligatory streaming show thing, where a non-conclusive ending is an entry to more seasons if the data shows enough viewer interest. But it would certainly be a more interesting creative choice to end the show here and let viewers stew in the ambiguity.

items.title: The Good Daughter Review
items.author: Matt Fowler
items.content:
This is a non-spoiler review for all six episodes of The Good Daughter, which premieres November 12 on Peacock.

Yes, another "Good" series has entered the chat (see also: Place, Wife, Fight, Doctor, Girls, more).

The Good Daughter, developed and written by Karin Slaughter and based on her own book, is an awesome Appalachian trauma drama. Starring Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy (The White Lotus, Drop) as estranged sisters, both lawyers, trying to get to the bottom of a high school shooting in their nasty, crooked Georgia hometown, the series is quite riveting. The main mystery, involving the aforementioned shooter, has a decent resolution, but it's the two sisters themselves, and a massively tragic shared event from their childhood, that infuses the show with complexity and poignancy.

As older sister Sam, Rose Byrne embodies a ferocious warmth amidst a shattered body.

The Peacock series has all the ingredients you need for a cracking small town whodunit, from a great ensemble to old family feuds to haunted secrets. It checks many boxes. And while it occasionally lapses into mystery genre cliches, it has enough unique subversive elements to keep it from getting stuck in the mud.

The two sisters, Sam and Charlie Quinn, are the heart and spine of the story, and what helps elevate it over many of its homespun crime peers. It's easy to see the trope-y architecture of one sister having abandoned the town for the big city and the other staying behind, or that the one who now resides in Manhattan is rigid and the one keeping the home fires burning is a wild child. But it's deeper than that. Byrne and Fahy are magnificent here as two women who are both, at once, right and wrong. Who are both justified and unreasonable. They deliver a palpable, gripping sibling relationship filled with recognizable pain, joy, and snark.

Byrne will be the star viewers are most familiar with here, having been in big spotlight projects ever since she broke through with American audiences on FX's Damages 20 years ago. As older sister Sam, Byrne embodies a ferocious warmth amidst a shattered body, all stemming from a nightmarish home invasion targeting her father when she was in high school. Sam is a living physical reminder of the fatal events that took her mother's life, as the show keenly dissects how people are often forced to reinvent their paths and plans and mourn their old selves. She's excellent, as usual.

Fahy is the anchor of the show, however, as The Good Daughter provides a wonderful opportunity to catch her in an incredible showcase performance. There's a chance you've seen her in past projects, but it wasn't until her Emmy nomination for The White Lotus that her profile truly lifted. And Blumhouse's ridiculous (but very fun) Drop from 2025 was also a great display of her talent. As younger sis Charlie, Fahy exhibits a vulnerable stubbornness, having grown up in the wake of a tragedy afraid to let those around her know just how much it damaged and affected her for fear of taking up space in front of those who suffered more. Charlie stayed behind, in fictional Pikeville, GA, despite Sam's attempts to wrestle her free, following in her father's footsteps as a local defense attorney-slash-pariah. She's the catalyst for the story, and also, in a way, its endgame.

The Quinn family exists in the crosshairs of their witch hunt-y neighbors, often maligned for father Rusty's legal defense of those guilty of heinous crimes. Brendan Gleeson's Rusty is a gem of an erudite, boozy blowhard. Easy to love, hard to live with, he's sly, steadfast, and plays the role of the fool as tactic. He rushes to the aid of teen Kelly (Shayna Benardo) after she's arrested for gunning down her principal and a classmate not because he thinks she's innocent, but because he knows the particulars of Pikeville and how ghoulish and corrupt the local mechanisms are.

Sisters Charlie and Sam entertain Rusty's latest bootless errand, and this is how our major players all converge. Still, though, it's past revelations that allow The Good Daughter to thrive. The Quinns' reunion comes with therapy, clarity, and the ghosts of that fateful afternoon, decades earlier, when everyone's life shattered. This offers up the true stratigraphy of The Good Daughter.

The surrounding ensemble is also worthy of praise, from Harper Steele's trusty, sassy office manager to Michael Dorman's reliable, loving ex-hubbie to Jake McDorman's hunky local color. They, along with the rest, are always two steps to the side of being standard mystery players, constantly offering up more than expected. If you pay attention to casting, and know your character actors, then you might be able to predict the outcome of the case, but still, that being said, there are many more reveals, especially pertaining to the the Sisters Quinn, that will outshine that.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3, Episodes 1-4 Review and Recap
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Some spoilers for Episodes 1-4 of Season 3 and past seasons of follow. Episodes 1-4 are available on Prime Video now, with Episodes 5 and 6 debuting on Nov. 18, and Episodes 7 and 8 finishing out the season on Nov. 25.

Season 3 refocuses The Rings of Power on its simple yet compelling good vs. evil premise, jettisoning some past characters and subplots while ensuring the ones remaining all align with the same goal: you exist to either defeat Sauron or to serve him.

Season 3 refocuses Rings of Power on its simple yet compelling good vs. evil premise, jettisoning some past characters and subplots while ensuring the ones remaining all align with the same goal.

Celebrimbor’s death last season means The Dark Lord (Charlie Vickers) isn’t having an easy time forging the One Ring. (Nice touch having Sauron keep Celebrimbor’s skeleton hanging around so his “ghost” – actor Charles Edwards returns for a cameo – can psychoanalyze him about his self-doubts.) Sauron desperately wants to discover whatever secret element Celebrimbor put into the Elven rings, as the Elves have thus far been able to stave off Sauron’s army at the borders of Lindon and Rivendell while nearly everywhere else in Middle-earth has fallen. To aid him in his quest to capture the Elven rings and discern their magic, Sauron has been busy turning mortal men into Nazgûl, promising them eternal life in exchange for becoming his servants of the ring.

Meanwhile, Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) have been busy battling the Orcs (and humans) that Sauron sends after them. Although she hasn’t encountered him in five years, Galadriel is beginning to feel Sauron’s presence again (Robert Aramayo’s Elrond thinks she’s just being paranoid). Galadriel’s past is briefly but sweetly explored here when she meets her future husband, Celeborn (a stalwart , back to being a pretty boy following years of Vecna ugliness), during a flashback to the First Age, where they court each other in a wire-fu duel reminiscent of Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon.

This sequence, when contrasted with the hardened warrior Galadriel has become, reveals how much she’s changed over a thousand years and the toll the conflict has taken on her. Morfydd Clark’s nuanced performance adeptly captures Galadriel's evolution from romantic to badass in just a few moments of screen time.

While the ongoing conflict between Sauron and the Elves is the main focus of Season 3, the first four episodes also catch viewers up with the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm, led by now-King Durin IV (Owain Arthur). While there’s some strained humor with the Dwarves, things get interesting with the arrival of Durin’s older brother, Thrain (the always compelling Eddie Marsan, who, even under a mound of makeup, proves an intriguing screen presence). Thrain has an agenda of his own that, by Episode 304, pits brother against brother for control of the dwarf kingdom. Durin and Disa’s (Sophia Nomvete) marriage is put to the test when a misstep from her past comes up, resulting in one of the strongest and most emotional scenes between the two in the whole series thus far.

In addition to Celeborn and Thrain, Season 3 also introduces another curious new addition to the cast in Marnûkh (Adam Young), who initially seems like a willing soldier of Sauron’s but ends up having a more complicated role to play. Marnûkh’s presence puts Galadriel and Arondir’s feelings about Orcs to the test, ultimately leading to tragedy by the end of Episode 304.

Speaking of which, Season 3 also gives Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), who has not always proved the most interesting character in this show, an Anakin-style arc. A grown man now, Theo has been enslaved by the Númenoreans the last five years, so when a chance presents itself for him to rebel against them – even if it means possibly becoming a Ringwraith for Sauron – he seizes it. This pays off hints that Theo was meant for the dark side that were first seeded in Season 1 when he found that broken sword hilt bearing the sigil of Sauron. He’s a bad guy now but, as with Anakin Skywalker, perhaps redemption is still possible for Theo in the end.

David Weyman’s Gandalf has more of the qualities we associate with the lovable wizard this season, and by Episode 4 his backstory and connection to Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard is revealed (thanks to a Moses-like chat with The Sacred Fire), setting up a more interesting challenge for Gandalf than simply having to battle a fellow sorcerer. I’ll be interested to see how that plays out in the remaining quartet of episodes.

I found the Númenor storyline less compelling than the other plot threads explored in Season 3’s first four episodes, but that’s been my least favorite storyline of the series since Season 1. Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) is a political creature and he has always struck me as a player better suited for a historical drama about intrigue at the royal court than in this particular fantasy tale. He’s a Westeros power player dropped into Middle-earth and whenever the story dwells too long in Númenor, I yearn for it to get back to literally any other character’s plot line.

That said, Ema Horvath’s Eärien gets a key episode this season that realigns her with her father Elendil (Lloyd Owen) and brothers Isildur (Maxim Baldry) and Anárion’s (Andrew Richardson) cause. Given how she broke with them at the end of Season 2, how and why Eärien is now working as their spy goes unexplored (for now). Was that always the case and she was on a long-term undercover mission? Or did she finally see the light after being married to Pharazôn? That remains unclear to me.

And while the first four episodes of Season 3 still offer their share of action (sword fights, arrows, etc.), any grand-scale battles are apparently being held for later in the season once Sauron’s quest to forge the One Ring inches him closer to victory. With the latest trailer teasing a Balrog battle and Sauron wearing the One Ring, I fully expect the latter half of Season 3 to start ramping up the action to epic levels.

items.title: We Build The Massive, Multi-Set LEGO Harry Potter Hogwarts Castle, Currently In Progress
items.author: Kevin Wong
items.content:
In 2024, LEGO began the most ambitious build project the company has ever attempted: a fully realized, minifigure-scale re-creation of Hogwarts Castle, made famous by the Harry Potter franchise. A single set of this size and scope would be impractically large and prohibitively expensive. So instead, LEGO is releasing numerous smaller LEGO Harry Potter sets that, when combined, will form the full castle. It's a truly massive undertaking.

This is an ongoing project; LEGO has not announced the end date for the final set. But we've been building the LEGO Hogwarts Castle since it launched, and we will continue building and adding to it until it's complete. If you would like to do the same? it's not too late to start, although LEGO retired some key sets at the end of 2025.

Here is every set released so far that comprises the modular LEGO Hogwarts Castle, currently in progress as of November 2026. You'll find a grand piece count and price count at the bottom, which I'll update as the castle continues to grow. Lastly, you can see some photos of the castle as it currently stands.

LEGO Harry Potter: Hogwarts Castle Sets

These are the sets you'll need to buy if you want to create your own enormous LEGO version of Hogwarts Castle. But these are just the sets released to date – more will be added in the future.

Hogwarts Castle: Owlery (Retired)

The Owlery is the first component of the Hogwarts Castle. If you're looking to cut a corner or two and save on costs, you might start with this one, because it's an independent structure apart from the main building. It has winter-themed, snow-capped spires, so if you're after aesthetic consistency, you might also want to swap out a few pieces to make the Owlery match seasons with the rest of the castle.

Hogwarts Castle: Boathouse (Retired)

Both the Boathouse and the Owlery share the same gray-colored hue on their spires. Back in 2024, this led many LEGO fans to speculate that these sets marked the beginning of a new Hogwarts Castle, even though it hadn't been officially announced yet. The Boathouse includes two small wooden boats, so you can recreate Harry's first-year arrival at Hogwarts.

Hogwarts Castle: Potions Class (Retired)

This is the first Hogwarts classroom set, which can swap in to replace another room in the castle. To use an example: The Great Hall comes with the girl's bathroom in the dungeon, where the troll attacks Hermione in the first book/movie. It's nice looking diorama, but it's extremely scene specific, and it doesn't really fit in with the rest of the castle. So, if you want to, you can swap out the troll scene with Professor Snape's Potions Classroom, which is a lot more detailed and colorful, and contains a wider range of roleplay opportunities. If you don't get the Potions Classroom, it's not going to look, at least outwardly, like something's missing. But still, it's hard to imagine Hogwarts without it.

Hogwarts Castle: The Great Hall (Retired)

The first major 'essential' building block in the Hogwarts Castle, the Great Hall includes the eponymous Hall – where the Sorting Ceremonies and Start and End-of-Term Feasts take place – and three additional rooms: the girl's bathroom where the troll attacked Hermione; a narrow corridor; and the Hufflepuff Common Room. The Great Hall connects to the Boathouse at the bottom of the outer stairwell; connects to the Main Tower at its side; and can swap its bathroom with the Potions Classroom. We built and photographed this one at the time of its launch.

Hogwarts Castle: Dueling Club (Retired)

This set recreates the Dueling Club scene from Chamber of Secrets, in which Draco conjures a snake and Harry uses Parseltongue to stop it from attacking Justin Finch-Fletchley. There's a gimmicked floor in the table that makes the minifigures fly backwards off of it. If you want, you can swap out the house tables in the Great Hall with the Dueling Club table. It's a fun alternative, but overall inessential to the larger castle, if that's what you're going for.

Hogwarts Castle: Charms Class

Professor Flitwick's Charms Classroom lets you recreate the Wingardium Leviosa scene from the first book/movie ("It's Levi-O-sa! Not Levio-SA."). The Professor Flitwick minifigure has his original movie appearance, when the filmmakers leaned into his goblin hertitage. The Charms Classroom slots into the Flying Lessons set, and can swap with the Quidditch equipment room.

Hogwarts Castle: Flying Lessons

On the exterior, this set depicts the scene where Harry rides a broom for the first time (it even includes a minifigure of Madame Hooch). But on the interior, this is a Professor McGonagall-centric set. It includes the aforementioned Quidditch equipment room, but it also contains McGonagall's office and McGonagall's Transfiguration classroom. The Flying Lessons set doesn't connect to any of the current sets; it'll fit in later, once we have more of the Castle completed.

Hogwarts Castle: Herbology Class

The Herbology Classroom includes a rare Professor Sprout minifigure, plus Hermione and Neville in their greenhouse smocks and gloves. The greenhouse feels appropriately overgrown and busy, with three mandrake plants and accompanying earmuff accessories. It is a freestanding structure from the larger Hogwarts Castle, although unlike the Owlery, it'll be in close proximity to it.

Hogwarts Castle: The Main Tower

The second major Hogwarts Castle set, the Main Tower connects directly to the Great Hall on its left side. And taken together (see more photos below), you really get a sense of size and scope. The interior contains three of the rooms from the Sorcerer's Stone trials: the Devil's Snare room, the Flying Keys room, and the Chess Set room. One floor up is Fluffy's room and a narrow corridor. One floor up from that is the Gryffindor Common Room. And then the actual Main Tower contains three staircases (two of them rotate), Dumbledore's office, and a secret room containing the Mirror of Erised. We built and photographed this set at launch.

Hogwarts Castle: Room of Requirement

This may end up being the rarest set in the whole modular collection. This re-creation of the Room of Requirement, as seen in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, includes hammocks and sleeping arrangements for Dumbledore's Army members. It comes with a single minifigure of Neville Longbottom.

The above price of $19.99 is what LEGO listed on their website. It was, however, never on sale by itself; rather, it was a gift-with-purchase for anyone who bought $130 worth of Harry Potter LEGO in the first week of September 2025. Your best bet is the secondary market, but don't break the bank over it; it's an an optional classroom that slots into the Main Tower, rather than a standing structure by itself.

Hogwarts Castle: Hospital Wing

A mandatory set for the full castle build, the Hospital Wing connects to the Main Tower and wraps around its right hand side. It contains far more than Madam Pomfrey's triage center, however; it also contains the Ravenclaw common room and Professor Lupin's Defense Against the Dark Arts classroom, complete with a Boggart wardrobe and phonograph.

Hogwarts Castle: Sorting Hat Ceremony

This set reimagines the Sorting Hat Ceremony as a wheel-spinning game, and it includes the hourglasses of rubies, diamonds, sapphires, and emeralds that tally the annual house points. It is designed to fit into the Great Hall as an add-on option, similar to the retired Dueling Club set. For fans looking to build the full castle, it's fun but ultimately inessential.

Hogwarts Castle: East Wing

An essential component to the overall build, the East Wing connects to both the Great Hall and the Main Tower via bridges. This set contains the Slytherin common room and Moaning Myrtle's batroom; go down a slide, and you'll wind up in the Chamber of Secrets. In addition to the massive, sculpted head of Salazar Sytherin, the Chamber of Secrets also features a scary-looking basilisk, which threatens to attack and kill all Muggle-born. The set includes 13 minifigures in all.

For photos of the entire Hogwarts Castle build so far, see below.

What's The Current Total Piece Count?

As of November 2026, the current total piece count stands at 9,778.

What's The Current Total Price?

As of November 2026, the current total price stands at $1162.87.

How Do You Put This All Together?

In the below photo, I've put together the entire castle, as of August 2026.

I've taken some creative license with the placement of the Hospital Wing. According to LEGO, it's supposed to form a courtyard at a right angle with the Main Tower. But it's impossible to see it, all the way back there, when you're looking at the castle from the front. I could display the castle from a different angle. But if I do this, it reveals the open backs of the models, which breaks the illusion.

So, I've decided to move the Hospital Wing to the area on the right side of the East Wing, directly above where I placed the Greenhouse. If the LEGO designers eventually put the Divination Tower or the Bell Towers in this area, I'll have to move the Hospital Wing again. But until then, I like how its current placement gives the castle better balance and makes it more physically imposing.

I've placed the Flying Lessons and the Owlery on the right side of the castle as well.

Just prior to releasing the Owlery, LEGO released an architectural build of Hogwarts Castle in miniature form. It has the same grey spires as the modular castle, and because of its timing, my theory is that it is a rough blueprint for how the final castle will look. Above, I've circled the parts of the modular castle that have been released. So, as you can see, we have about one-third of the final building to go.

Still, some LEGO fans have theorized that the Hogwarts Castle is complete. The reasoning is that the old 6,020-piece microscale build stopped at the East Wing and never built beyond that.

In May 2026, I reached out to LEGO and asked them if the East Wing marked the end of the castle build. They got back to me, stating that they weren't able to share information regarding that.

It definitely feels like the designers could go further if they wanted to. The three most notable, missing parts of the castle are the Astronomy Tower, the Clock Tower, and the Bell Towers. We are almost certainly not getting the Clock Tower because of its canonical placement behind the Main Tower. The Bell Towers are a slight possibility. But the Astronomy Tower would be the most likely (and desirable) of the three.
