She is saved through her own skill and the help of enigmatic and handsome Prince Heinrey (Romance is a Bonus Book’s Lee Jong-suk), when he is in his secondary form as a bird; yes, a bird. These glimpses at magical world-building are intriguing, but don’t pay off in any cohesive way in the first act of the season.

The momentum suggested in the first episode does build when Prince Heinrey properly enters the narrative in his human form. In the first few episodes, he fosters a relationship with Navier solely as a bird, delivering messages to the empress from a mysterious admirer (i.e. him). In these encounters, the notorious ladies’ man begins to fall for the beautiful and lonely Navier. While Navier begins to see the bird as a confidante, she does not yet know that the creature she cares for and shares her secrets with is actually a human man, let alone the next in line for the throne of the Western Kingdom.

When Heinrey-as-human finally arrives at the Eastern Empire court, along with nobility from other empires for a New Year’s Celebration, The Remarried Empress utilizes some killer historical-romance-on-screen shorthands to great effect. When Navier and Heinrey share a dance in a ballroom of their royal social circle, it builds on the cinematic language crafted by Pride and Prejudice adaptations and recently utilized by Bridgerton to instantly communicate authentic, romantic intimacy. More broadly, the charismatic irreverence of Prince Heinrey’s character brings a much-needed levity to the self-serious triangle of Navier, Sovieshu, and Rashta, and his instant devotion to Navier gives us something more substantial to root for.

The interplay between these four main characters is helped immensely by the quality of this cast and by the lavish production design and setting. The Remarried Empress seemingly spared no expense in bringing the fantasy romance to the screen. Unlike most Korean historical fantasy dramas, Remarried Empress' palace setting is inspired by European architecture, fashion, and etiquette, and was filmed in the Czech Republic and Germany to capture a Western aesthetic. This blend of a Western-inspired fantasy setting with a Korean cast and story sensibility gives The Remarried Empress a unique watchability, even if it doesn’t have anything particularly interesting to say about power or politics thus far.

In a global streaming landscape that takes so few big swings on romantasy series, we can’t be too hasty about dismissing a series like The Remarried Empress.

The Remarried Empress also benefits greatly from the current dearth of big-budget romantasy series. Despite the massive success of book series like A Court of Thorns and Roses, we have gotten so few big-budget TV shows in the genre, which speaks to Hollywood’s broader devaluing of romance-centric storytelling over the past few decades and women as our own audience. While this is beginning to change in no small part due to the massive, proven success of Korean dramas around the world, we have yet to see a breakout hit. Netflix’s Shadow and Bone had immense potential, but was canceled (despite its strong viewership) before getting to the main Six of Crows storyline, widely considered to be the meatiest part of Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse; I still lament.

So far, The Remarried Empress is nowhere near as good as Six of Crows, though it might be on par with Shadow and Bone; I hope it gets a chance to evolve in a way the Shadow and Bone adaptation never did. In a global streaming landscape that takes so few big swings on romantasy series, we can’t be too hasty about dismissing a series like The Remarried Empress. In its first four episodes, it has yet to live up to the potential of the immense creative and financial resources invested in it, but what’s a princess story for if not believing in a happier ending?

items.title: The Cat in the Hat (2026) Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Having received a 2003 live-action adaptation that , the Cat in the Hat is back with a new feature film. This time, it’s in animated form, and fortunately the end result is a much better one.

With Mike Myers having starred in the live-action version, another group of filmmakers have once more turned to a Saturday Night Live alum, with Bill Hader now voicing the Cat. Dr. Seuss's beloved children's book is far too short to make for a feature-length story on its own, so things are rather drastically reinterpreted and expanded upon here, with writer-directors Erica Rivinoja (South Park, Borat Subsequent Moviefilm) and Alessandro Carloni (Kung Fu Panda 3) essentially just taking the basic idea of the fantastical Cat in the Hat appearing to children to encourage imagination and mischief.

The opening scenes feel somewhat similar to Monsters, Inc., establishing an entire imagination-based business of sorts with the Cat in the Hat as an employee. Other anthropomorphic animals work alongside him, all in the service of providing entertainment and encouragement to kids needing an imagination boost. Fortunately, the film doesn’t get too bogged down in the “company” scenario, mostly using it as a fun way to incorporate nods to the Seuss-y source material in the form of rhyming rules explained by staff members (voiced by the likes of Giancarlo Esposito, Bowen Yang, and Quinta Brunson), along with some visual depictions of the Cat in that Hat that also harken back to the book. From there, the story follows the Cat appearing to sister and brother Gabby (Xochitl Gomez) and Sebastian (Tiago Martinez), who are trying to deal with moving to a new city with their mother, Carmen (America Ferrera).

The Cat in the Hat shows genuine creativity from the start, beginning with its distinct visual interpretation of its two worlds. The realm the Cat and his colleagues live in appears much more bright, colorful, and off-kilter compared to the more realistic and muted feel given to Gabby and Sebastian’s apartment life. The film thankfully provides solid laughs on a fairly frequent basis too, from sight gags and slapstick that can entertain all ages to some notably multilayered jokes that can easily work for kids but arguably hit harder for the adults in the audience.

It also certainly helps to have Bill Hader voicing the Cat, bringing his deft sense of humor to the role along with his ability to do impressive voices. In addition to Hader, the movie has a bit of a cheat code in the form of Matt Berry (What We Do in the Shadows) as the voice of Gabby and Sebastian's pet fish, Waffles, who the Cat promptly gives the ability to speak. Is there a greater and more innately funny voice than Berry's these days? Hearing his bombastic delivery as an overwhelmed and frustrated fish is continually funny.

The film’s storyline involves the Cat introducing and then promptly losing a device that functions in a manner similar to Doctor Strange's Time Stone, enabling the user to rewind recent events. The search for this device takes the Cat, Gabby, and Sebastian inside incredible versions of the moving boxes that still fill the kids’ apartment; they travel through worlds where everything inside these boxes appears larger than life, often having actually come to life in the form of various toys, objects, and drawings they encounter. While some of this is a bit reminiscent of the journey through the mind in Inside Out, there are a lot of unique and appreciated touches throughout as everything from musical instruments to IKEA instructions can and do express themselves in various ways.

Despite overstaying its welcome, The Cat in the Hat remains easy to enjoy thanks to its likability and humor.

The one big drawback with the film is that it’s simply too long for its subject matter, losing energy as it nears its conclusion. Running just a few minutes shy of two hours, it starts to drag in its third act; an obvious reason for this is that there are just too many overlapping conflicts introduced. The film is ultimately juggling the Cat’s quest to get back his lost device; a monstrous creature called “Something” who is pursuing our heroes; the fact that the Cat in the Hat's job is in jeopardy thanks to recent screw-ups; and another subplot about Carmen’s snooping landlord (Paula Pell), who is itching for a reason to evict the new family in the building thanks to her strict rules. It feels like Rivinoja and Carloni overcompensated for how slight the book is; the movie would have been better served by dropping at least one of these storylines, as the movie feels noticeably stretched out as it nears its resolution.

Still, despite overstaying its welcome, The Cat in the Hat remains easy to enjoy thanks to its likability and humor. That includes how it makes use of the book’s popular Thing 1 and Thing 2 characters, who are expanded here into a large group of similar Thing creatures that the Cat unleashes into Gabby and Sebastian’s apartment. These weird little guys have an amusing and wacky Gremlins-type chaotic energy, even as you can feel the studio salivating at the chance to turn the Things into the next Minions. But being aware of that is made easier when you’re watching an often sly film like The Cat in the Hat, which provides its own very good meta joke that acknowledges this fact with a wink.

items.title: Wild Horse Nine Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Two killers head out on a not quite break-from-work trip to a picturesque location, where shenanigans ensue. I've seen that movie and it's called In Bruges, you might be saying. But In Bruges writer-director Martin McDonagh is far from playing the same Funny Games as Michael Haneke by making the same film twice, so while his new film Wild Horse Nine might put him in familiar territory, this is not just another In Bruges -- and we are all the better for it.

The Catholic guilt remains, but McDonagh trades the tortured hitmen of In Bruges for two CIA spooks who need a reprieve from setting up Augusto Pinochet's coup in early '70s Chile. So off they go for a quick breather from working to overthrow a democratically elected Marxist (the CIA can't have that, no. Definitely not in their own hemisphere!) to see the big heads on Easter Island.

What makes this film great is its ability to tackle heady subjects like political violence and CIA-backed regime change and yet still be funny as hell and a great hangout movie. It's a tough needle to thread, but Martin McDonagh does it without being insensitive to the real-world changes that are happening around his characters.

Petty. Brilliant. Bickering.

McDonagh is an excellent filmmaker, but he’s undoubtedly best at screenwriting. His dialogue is incredible. It can be absurd, funny, charming, mean, and insightful; most of the time, it can be all of those at once. I've been using some form of "You're a nice guy, Pádraic" as my preferred euphemism for calling people an idiot ever since I saw The Banshees of Inisherin. It's such a nice, pleasant veneer, but it's so cutting. And when I use it, most people don't realize I'm insulting them, just like Pádraic.

Wild Horse Nine is also chock-full of great zingers. Take the scene in the trailer, where Lee (Sam Rockwell) is trying to shush Chris (John Malkovich), who won't stop talking about all his political assassinations.

Chris snaps back, "I've killed people in countries you can't even spell," and then mentions that he killed a guy in Czechoslovakia.

"You never killed anyone in Czechosl-fucking-vakia. You just know I can't spell it," responds Lee.

Those micro-tugs-of-war for power, jockeying for a kind of dominance that's ultimately inconsequential, are a hallmark of McDonagh's writing and what make his dialogue so memorable. It's part lyrical, part petty, and even takes on elements of stand-up comedy like the callback.

For example, some of the film's best jokes are set up early with pithy lines, only to be paid off later. And in a true test of a film's quality, McDonagh didn't burn off the best moments of dialogue in the trailer.

Of course, McDonagh's dialogue is only half the equation. A script is only as good as the hands of the performers it's in, and McDonagh has assembled a great cast.

Sam Rockwell is back, collaborating with the director who helped him win his Oscar for 2018's Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. This time he's playing Lee, a spy whose loyalty is torn between his partner and his agency.

John Malkovich co-stars as Lee's partner and the more seasoned spy, Chris. The CIA was doing tons of meddling in the '60s and '70s, and Chris was boots on the ground for a lot of it. All that experience combined with his wildcard nature is what's pushing Steve Buscemi's MJ (the head of the CIA's South American operations) to believe he's a real liability and insist, "He ain't leaving the fuckin' island." (Can you blame the guy? He's talking about killing people... on an airplane.)

Listening to these two bicker is the absolute best part of the film.

Lee and Chris's relationship is a cockeyed mix of Obi-Wan and Anakin and part Riggs and Murtaugh. Malkovich's Chris is both the old, grizzled Murtaugh and the maverick Riggs combined into one CIA spy. Meanwhile, Lee is the well-meaning Padawan who is on the verge of having to make some hard decisions.

Whether Chris is pontificating on why "gay countries make the best cheese" or clowning on Lee for all his wife's infidelities, Malkovich has most of the film's best lines. (Speaking of which, Parker Posey is absolutely hilarious as Lee's wife Margie.) Listening to these two bicker is the absolute best part of the film. That's all thanks to Malkovich and Rockwell's chemistry, which makes these scenes feel like the effortless banter of old colleagues.

Quips aside, Malkovich deftly handles a complex, multifaceted character with empathy and charm. Without getting into too much detail, Chris knows he isn't long for this world, and, like the flawed Catholic he is, he's seeking a bit of redemption on his way out. He's said some bad things, done some worse things; his ability to piss off literally every character in the film is unrivaled. But Malkovich's charisma keeps us invested in him, and by the end, we're rooting for him.

The film's redemptive tension is best exemplified by Chris's relationship with Monica, one of the young progressive women he insults at the airport. Played by Chilean actress Mariana di Girolamo, Monica is essentially the heart of the film. Despite being completely repulsed by Chris's antics, they keep running into each other on the island, and eventually it's Monica who really forces Chris to confront his past and draw out what's left of his humanity.

I can't help but compare this film to In Bruges. In many superficial ways, they're extremely similar, but the comparison also helps emphasize how much Martin McDonagh has improved as a storyteller. It's not like he was bad before; In Bruges, with its funny but generic hitmen on the lam, was one of the better aughts crime flicks that were trying to duplicate Pulp Fiction's success over a decade later.

Wild Horse Nine and In Bruges share themes of guilt, redemption, moral codes, and loyalty. But where In Bruges confines its moral reckoning to the personal, grounding Wild Horse Nine in historical events adds an extra layer of thematic depth. Using the lead-up to Pinochet's coup as the backdrop for Lee and Chris's misadventures on Easter Island forces the characters to confront the moral culpability of their actions, while also challenging American audiences to reckon with the enduring consequences of their country's political meddling.

To put a finer point on it, it's extremely tough for a film to have me laughing at two CIA agents debate who would be a bigger security risk to the agency, a boozer wife or a heroin wife, and also get me to wiki Patrice Lumumba immediately after walking out of the theater. But that's what makes Wild Horse Nine stand out: it makes the absurdity of these men entertaining without letting you forget the very real consequences of their work.

Cinematography That Evokes a '70s Aesthetic

If you're like me, you go see a Martin McDonagh film for the script and the performances. But make no mistake, Wild Horse Nine is a beautifully photographed film, even if there’s nothing outstanding about its cinematography. McDonagh and cinematographer Ben Davis really lean into the time period's '70s aesthetic. Some of the film's shots were made to look like they were came from Lee's Super 8 camera, and even have the edges of the stock in frame. The film's establishing shots, especially those featuring the island's iconic moai (the big heads), are rendered beautifully in a grainy, hypersaturated film stock.

Visually, the film makes the most out of its locations in the same way an Italian chef makes the most out of their ingredients. Bear with me here a second. Originally, I wanted to say the film's cinematography was too workmanlike, but that's too harsh. To better understand the film's photographic choices, we need to examine the differences between the philosophies of French and Italian cooking.

For those unaware, French cooking takes a more maximalist approach, emphasizing the chef's skill and the complex methods they use to prepare an ingredient, while Italian cooking emphasizes minimalism, drawing focus to the quality of an ingredient by preparing it using the simplest methods.

While McDonagh and Davis take the Italian chef approach to their framing, getting out of the way of some truly magnificent vistas, they still have some tricks up their sleeves, progressively increasing their use of close-ups as the film gets more and more intimate with the characters. Despite these almost subliminal techniques, the camerawork never really adds a level of flair that would make it stand out.

items.title: Bass X Machina Episode 1 Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Episode 1, “Until Then... I'm Bass Reeves.” The full six-episode season is available now on Netflix.

The latest animated production from (Devil May Cry, X-Men '97, My Adventures With Superman, etc.) to make its way to our airwaves… or streaming waves – whatever we’re calling them these days – Bass X Machina is, based on this first episode, a fun and violent excursion into the world of the steampunk Western, but with an eye to Black history. Or rather, alt-history, since this series gives us a Wild West where robots and cyborgs are the norm, even while the face-in-the-dirt killin’ remains as ruthless as ever.

Brian Tyree Henry, who also is an executive producer on the series, voices Bass Reeves, or this world’s version of Bass Reeves, who of course in reality was a historic lawman; an ex-slave who went on to become a Deputy U.S. Marshal, Reeves has been portrayed in movies, TV and elsewhere many times over the years, perhaps most notably in recent years in Damon Lindelof’s Watchmen (where his legend inspired that world’s first superhero, ).

As the first episode starts, Reeves explains in VO how, after the Civil War, the Union Army was “saddled with thousands of Black soldiers they didn’t know what to do with. And after having known the horrors of war, some of these soldiers didn’t know what to do with themselves.” Some chose the life of the gun in the West, some became Buffalo Soldiers, and “some legendary few… became lawmen.”

Only when we first meet Reeves, he’s a bounty hunter, not a lawman – a fact which is driven home immediately when he shoots two opponents without thinking twice about it. In fact, he’s also part machine, utilizing a steam-powered arm which has replaced his real appendage at some point in his violent history. Quick flashbacks/dreams to some blood-red past event indicate we’ll eventually learn the story of how he came by that arm, but not today.

The action in this first episode is fun and bloody, with a dynamic range of camera moves and angles as Reeves, for starters, shoots the heck out of a gang of crooks.

The action in this first episode is fun and bloody, with a dynamic range of camera moves and angles as Reeves, for starters, shoots the heck out of a gang of crooks during a train heist. Bullets enter (and exit) foreheads with style, while the speed of the racing train and pyrotechnics of a Gatling gun add to the overall excitement of the opening scene. Henry’s Reeves also establishes his general apathy towards his opponents right out of the gate, such as when, after dispatching one fellow’s two brothers, the man cries, “You took my brothers away!” Henry’s Reeves dispassionately responds, “You’re back with ‘em now” before finishing the guy off with a single shot. Dang.

After an opening credits sequence that further hints at Reeves’ origin story, complete with propulsive theme song by Janelle Monáe, the series’ main storyline is established. A scientist named Dr. Eugene Starr has gone missing, apparently into the Native American territory called the Badlands. But not just any scientist: It seems Starr, or someone close to him, has been experimenting on the “magic metal that’s going around” – and using it on people. Whether or not this magic metal is the same substance that has made “boilertech” commonplace in this world is unclear, but regardless, human experimentation is clearly a topic of interest for Reeves, who says that his arm “wasn’t lost. It was stolen.”

Tati Gabrielle voices Dana Starr, a young woman who is the niece of the missing scientist and an engineering genius who winds up playing sidekick to Reeves. She’s able to build handy gadgets while also calculating things like, say, how much time Dr. Starr has left to live after the possibility of “predation, murder, dysentery, despair.” (The answer is three days.) Monáe also voices Reeves’ wife Glory, and we learn that the couple have two sons as well. But Reeves can’t rest – or be a father and husband – while he knows that the key to his past could be lurking out there with Dr. Starr…

Created by LeSean Thomas, who’s also worked on series like Yasuke, Cannon Busters, and Black Dynamite, Bass X Machina finds a nice balance between the Western tropes, retro-sci-fi tech, bloody violence, and animated style. By the time Episode 1 winds down and Reeves and Dana are heading off into the Badlands to begin their journey – one on a horse and the other on a makeshift boilertech scooter – it’s clear that this has not just been the beginning of a beautiful friendship, but also of a cool new animated world.

items.title: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
The first time I ever saw Japan's most famous kaiju on the big screen was in Godzilla 2000: Millennium. Like any nine-year-old kid, I was obsessed with Big G. I read the Dark Horse comics, and I taped all the movies I could on TV. Things were different then; Godzilla was a big deal, but theatrical releases for Godzilla films were incredibly rare in the States If you saw those movies, it was on TV and they were dubbed or edited versions released under different titles like Godzilla: King of the Monsters or Godzilla vs. The Sea Monster. After Godzilla 2000 underperformed, it took another five years for the series to see a theatrical release in the U.S. – and into that void stomped 2002’s Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee.

It was the perfect mix of subject matter (big monsters who were super into professional wrestling), genre (3D fighting game), and time period (licensed games were still, like… a thing). It was the kind of game that could dominate a pizza-filled sleepover weekend or become your personality for an entire summer. One friend’s parents bought it for them, and that copy became communal: a holy thing, carried from place to place. Maybe it’s fitting that it’s back now in the form of Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered, 24 years later. The world (and Godzilla) has changed a lot, but original developer Pipeworks is still at the helm. It somehow feels just as relevant now as it did then, just in different ways, and revisiting it was a joy even removed from the nostalgia.

There is no one-to-one equivalent for what Destroy All Monsters Melee is, but the idea is pretty simple: you pick one of 12 monsters from Godzilla’s history (up through Godzilla 2000) – Godzilla, Gigan, Megalon, Ghidorah, etc. – then choose a real-world city or iconic Godzilla location to battle it out in. You’ll fight in classic rubber suit wrestling style while dodging environmental hazards, knocking down buildings, throwing rocks and skyscrapers at each other, and squashing the annoying military forces that really would prefer if you made a mess somewhere else. Last kaiju standing wins.

Despite the name, this isn't a straight remaster. You're not just looking at uprezzed models. It looks fantastic while also maintaining the “these are guys in rubber suits drop-kicking each other” vibe that defines the films it’s based on. The audio pulls its weight, too – the soundtrack has the booming authority you'd expect from a Godzilla film, buildings crumble and collapse spectacularly, beam attacks sound powerful and painful, the radio calls from military forces in the area let you know where they’ll be focusing their fire, and the announcer is having a blast. And the monsters, of course, sound like themselves. And yeah, Godzilla makes The Noise, just like you remember, even if it’s your first time here.

All of this is held together by a spit-and-duct-tape story that's just there to get you brawling: see, there's this alien race called the Vortaak. They're little green men with funky helmets, straight-from-the-‘50s fashion sense, flying saucers, and more than a little ego. They're here to take over the Earth, and what better way to do it than mind control the frankly absurd number of kaiju that are just hanging around, ready to smash a city at a moment's notice? Unfortunately for them, whichever Monster you pick breaks free of their mind control and decides the Earth is worth saving. Driving off the Vortaak means KOing the other monsters. All in a day's work, really.

The soundtrack has the booming authority you'd expect from Godzilla.

That's Adventure mode, which is one of several single-player options for you to rearrange cities in. You've also got Destruction for the score chasers, where you have to wreck a city in a time limit, a souped-up Adventure mode for monsters who are at a higher level and have better stats (which you gain from experience you earn as you play certain modes), and Survival, which is exactly what it sounds like.

Listen, you can count the number of fighting games with good single-player modes on two hands (and several of those have the words “Soul Calibur” in their titles), but what's on offer here is solid if not spectacular. You only start with four monsters and a few stages unlocked, but Pipeworks has smartly reworked this remaster so you can unlock the rest in pretty much whatever order you like. You just have to meet the requirements, which you do by playing, following rumors, and unlocking research, and you can swap what you're focusing on whenever you like.

On the one hand, yeah, it's super satisfying to unlock Ghidorah because it's Ghidorah – as soon as he stops being a silhouette I can't select and starts being a gloriously golden three-headed dragon I can take into battle, some lizard part of my brain gets very happy because I can't wait to fly around and shoot lightning with that sumbitch. On the other hand, it's mad annoying to see Rodan or Ghidorah or Mecha Godzilla in Adventure mode and have the 12-year-old who lives in my head put down his slice of pizza long enough to be like “hell yeah, I wanna play that one” and then realize I can't, especially in multiplayer. Does it give you more reasons to keep playing? Absolutely, and this stuff was part and parcel of the original experience. But man, sometimes you just wanna throw down with your friends without worrying about unlocks, you know?

Multiplayer, of course, is really what Destroy All Monsters Melee is designed for, and I'm so happy that Pipeworks has added online play in addition to the returning local options. It even works really well! Most of the matches I played pre-release were smooth, though I did suffer a few disconnects. (Almost all of which happened when I was winning or doing well – I'm not saying my boy Lucas is a fraud or anything, but…)

It's here, in the multiplayer, that Destroy All Monsters Melee really shines. People will tell you, naively, that this is a button masher with no depth. These people are foolish and wrong, and if this were a Godzilla movie, they'd got a dramatic close-up shot right before a giant monster foot turned them into paste. Can you play a chaotic four-player free-for-all where everybody is mashing? Sure. You can also do wacky team battles or square off against the never-as-challenging-as-another-person CPU (though, bafflingly, you can't mix CPU opponents with friends online; let me do a comp stomp, man!). This can certainly be a casual party game if you want it to be.

But the thing about Destroy All Monsters Melee is that there is actually quite a bit more to it. Each monster has punch, kick, and fierce attacks that you can string into combos. Tilt the left stick in a direction and you get heavy attacks. Every kaiju has an energy attack governed by an energy bar that you can use as a quick projectile or charge for a beam. You can also pick up and throw buildings and rocks, or even other kaiju. You can run, jump, fly (if your character has wings), crouch, and block.

This can be a casual party game, but there is actually quite a bit more to its combat.

All of this opens up most of the stuff you'd see in a traditional fighting game. Someone shoot a projectile at you? Duck it. If you've knocked another monster down, they can wake up with an attack, but if you block it or stand just outside of their range, you can punish them instead. Finishing a predictable string when an opponent is blocking means you are either getting hit or thrown for your trouble.

Every monster also has different stats to account for. Gigan's sword arms mean he hits… well, like a kaiju with sword arms, but his projectiles are relatively weak. Anguirus can't block normally, but his spiked shell means anyone who hits him while his back is turned is gonna be dancing around in a lot of pain. Megalon can burrow and come up under you. And Godzilla 2000's additional bit of quickness means he can apply pressure a lot more easily than his ‘90s counterpart. Knowing what the other city smasher you're staring down can do matters, and someone who understands the difference between Blunt and Edge attacks or who knows when to duck your strings is going to beat your colossal ass up and down Tokyo Bay if you're just mashing.

But smart map play matters, too. Once you start to destroy a city, there's less cover to hide behind in future rounds and fewer things to throw at your opponent. It also means it’s easier to make a beeline for the power-ups that drop on the map – like Rage, which buffs your character and provides access to powerful Rage attacks. There are health and energy boosts, as well as my personal favorite, the Mothra Airstrike, which the announcer proclaims with a relish that makes me think he's been waiting to see a giant moth divebomb another kaiju his whole life. If you break down cliffs on Monster Island, you can chuck another monster into the lava. Crack open the forcefield on the alien’s Mothership and there's a whole other part of the stage to fight in. It's good stuff.

Is it as deep as Street Fighter or Guilty Gear of Tekken? No. But a lot goes into a match of Destroy All Monsters Melee, and knowing your kaiju goes a long way. There is replay value in filling out the gallery and score chasing in Destruction Mode, but if you vibe with what's here, it will be because you love it. And by “it,” I mean uppercutting a monster the size of the Chrysler Building and watching him hang in the air for a second before he comes crashing back down to Earth.

Admittedly, the deeper stuff isn't easy to learn because Destroy All Monsters Melee barely teaches you any of it. Aside from loading screen text and a basic movelist, there is no tutorial of any kind, so I learned by trial and error, talking to the people I was playing with, and hunting down guides for the original game. That sucks, because the fun part is digging into these systems, and it's much more fun when you understand the layers hidden beneath the scales (or metal).

I came out of Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered with my brain rewired – or maybe more accurately, it reminded me of what's important. It's not how big the roster is or whether there's a progression system to keep you playing forever once the character unlocks run out. It’s not about achievements or daily quests or a battle pass or all the other useless Skinner Box nonsense crammed into everything these days. This is a time capsule, a pure reminder that what makes a game are the moments at 2 a.m. when you throw your buddy into the lava pit… which happens to have a Rage power up in it. It's the comebacks and the laughs. It's like stepping back into the shoes of my nine-year-old self, seeing a Godzilla film in theaters before the series was drowning in cultural clout and an interconnected multimedia universe. The joy is in the thing itself. In surrendering your expectations and remembering how things can make you feel if you let them. Everything else is noise. And not the cool Godzilla kind.

items.title: Monster Hunter Outlanders Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
If there's a singular idea that defines Monster Hunter, it's the grind. Capcom's mega-hit franchise, ever since its inception on the PSP, has flourished because of how it embraces the very idea of grinding and transforms it into an infectiously fun gameplay loop. Repetition and habit are vital parts of the series, so it makes sense, then, that the mobile game gacha format would eventually come to Monster Hunter, fitting currencies and timed gauges into that collecting and grinding experience. But my biggest surprise with Monster Hunter Outlanders has been how it's a comprehensive, full-fledged Monster Hunter packed onto phones and tablets. While it does eventually get buried under an avalanche of currencies to keep track of and some gacha roadblocks, there's enough meat on the bone here to sustain those hungry for more Monster Hunter or a solid action RPG on mobile.

Like most Monster Hunter games, Outlanders follows a group of intrepid explorers from the Adventurer's Guild, this time sent to the uncharted island of Aesolan to investigate a mineral called Radiantate, and how it's influencing various breeds of monsters. After a brief action-packed intro, you're essentially let loose onto the island, free to explore the first environment or tackle the story as you see fit. But also, like most Monster Hunter games, the initial 20 or so hours of Outlanders are extremely guided and layered with seemingly endless tutorials. That's compounded by the nature of being a mobile game, meaning it has to introduce a half-dozen modes, various pull systems, currencies for powering up your Adventurer, and much more.

The most succinct way to describe Outlanders is if you took Monster Hunter World, streamlined its combat, and crammed the entire thing into a mobile game. I almost cannot overstate how closely Outlanders resembles World in every way, even right down to the general structure and story. It takes a bit of an interesting approach, filling the story with a cast of characters that doubles as the big gacha pulls, even though you also have your "main" player-created character. While the overall story feels a bit rote and generic, the world of Outlanders itself is still brimming with things to do. While not a traditional open world game, it's in the exact same framework as Monster Hunter World and Wilds, giving you massive zones to explore. In these zones, you can naturally hunt monsters (without kicking off missions), gather resources, engage in little minigames like a rhythmic one where you steal a flying monster's treasure, and undertake any number of sidequests.

My biggest surprise with Outlanders is how uncompromising the scope of its world feels, right in line with a big mainline Monster Hunter, supported by the fact that this game looks absolutely stunning, and runs like a dream. On an iPhone 14 Plus I was able to run the game on High settings with a stable 45fps, and almost zero slowdown, even during intense battles.

The actual act of exploring the world feels just as entrancing as in major Monster Hunters. Various options for constructing camps and equipment as you explore the world make both traversal and item gathering easier. Camps unlock fast travel points and places to rest, catapults send your adventurer flying on their glider at high speed, and resource collectors constantly soak up those valuable items you need.

Combat is still largely about that push-and-pull of timing, knowing when to pivot between offense and defense, and winding up your attacks at just the right time. That timing and weight of battle has always set Monster Hunter apart from other action games, and it's still present here. But where you can see the mobile limitations is in the particulars of combat control and the various, and many systems, used to improve your Adventurer's stats.

Essentially, Outlanders is a squad-based Monster Hunter, where you build a party consisting of your main character and characters you pull (multiplayer with other actual players is available, too). But you can also play as each of the gacha characters, who have their own movesets, Ultimates, and abilities. For example, Keres uses dual blades that are actually a set of claws, giving her a completely separate set of skills, including one Wolverine-like drill attack. Meanwhile, Luxheart has a two-handed sword that he can rev up to shoot out fireworks, making each of his attacks like a miniature show. These various characters are actually one of my favorite parts of Outlanders, as their designs dig into a bit of , leaning into the overall goofiness of Monster Hunter as well.

The smart streamlining of combat still keeps the intensity of hunts alive, while being more playable in short bursts.

Having distinct movests also goes a long way to breaking up the monotony of repeat hunts and grinding. However, Outlanders overall has fewer weapon types than the last few games as a result, clocking in at eight total weapon types – some notable exclusions being the Hunting Horn and Insect Glaive. And overall, Outlanders plays a bit like a slightly simplified version of World in that it streamlines the more dynamic gameplay. For example, a lot of the emergent world elements, like using a Flashfly to stun a monster, are simple icons that pops up on-screen if you're near.

The bigger change, however, is Outlander's two different control schemes: Adventure and Classic. Adventure boils everything down to three buttons – Attack, React, and Burst – automatically and intuitively altering each of these buttons based on the situation. As examples, the Bowgun will swap ammo based on what's most effective in the moment, or the react button might turn into a guard instead of a dodge.

Classic control mode gives you more fine-tuned control with more dedicated buttons in the vein of a typical Monster Hunter experience. It works fine on a touchscreen, perhaps even a bit better than I was expecting. But if you opt to use touch controls, I'd heavily recommend the Adventure control scheme, simply because Classic is a lot to juggle without a gamepad-style attachment or accessory. I did find the best way to play Outlanders is on Classic with a controller, but of course, that may not be an option for everyone all the time.

Another piece of good news is that Outlanders still shines in terms of monster designs and variety, and that's essential to get right. There's a good array of creatures from across the series, and each monster gets a second souped-up "Radiant" form that adds new attacks and behaviors you need to contend with. Outlanders also still has that wonderful emergent element of World and Wilds where an even bigger predator might stumble into the middle of your battle, forcing you to adapt on the fly.

The simplified control scheme and combat does mean some big changes in how you approach fighting monsters. While you can still climb walls by running up to them, there is no dedicated jump action so you're largely relegated to the ground in fights. Ultimates and skills from your partner characters, like cannons that shoot nets, help add more to the ground game – but sometimes I just wish I could jump on a Rathalos' tail for those thrilling moments I enjoy from the series. By and large, that more streamlined combat experience works for what Outlanders is going for: little snippets and bursts of satisfying gameplay, maybe one quest on the train, or while you're waiting in line somewhere.

A lot of the core systems of Outlanders click together well, but obviously, the bigger question is how the monetization and gacha systems work. As I said earlier, Monster Hunter has always been about grinding, but finding unique ways to make that grind enjoyable. Unfortunately, Outlanders doesn't always succeed at that second part. When I say the currency and overarching systems of this game can be confusing, I really mean it. I'm no stranger to gacha games, I've seen their evolution over the two decades I've been playing them, but even I had a hard time keeping track of everything I had to juggle in Outlanders.

On top of equipment and partners (like Palicos) for each adventurer, you also have to upgrade their charms, and then ascend said charms once you've reached max level. But in order to boost the max level, you need to raise your Ecological Rank, which also has a number of different requirements. Not to mention that partners have their own leveling system. Then there's the Insight system that adds skills to each adventurer based on skill points they've accrued with weapons. Then there's the Visage system, where you need to "paint" cards of the monsters you take down in the world, as you defeat them. Multiple Visages can be equipped on each character, and every Visage can be ranked up individually.

Oh yeah, and there's Adventurer Rank, Proof of Mastery level, and Investigation Notes – all of which are sort of independent levelling and knowledge systems. Then there are rewards for the specific season the game is on, and different launch initiatives that also have their own currency to gain (and many have optional passes you can purchase for real money to get more rewards). There are a few different gameplay modes on top of all this. You can, of course, follow the main story and simply explore the world. But outside of that, you can take on Free Hunts for specific monsters, use rechargeable Stamina for Hunt Requests to gain levelling items, a lengthy Trial Expedition mode where you take on 150 battles of ascending difficulty, and Guild Clash and Guild Carnival modes where different guilds play together.

Needless to say, there's a metric ton of things to do in Outlanders, and even across 30 hours of playing this game you'll be unlocking new modes, tutorials, and options. If these systems were complementary to that core hunting experience it'd be one thing, but so often Outlanders' deluge of systems simply gets in the way of the action, grinding things down to a halt as you trudge through menus.

Outlanders' deluge of systems simply gets in the way of the action, grinding things down to a halt as you trudge through menus.

To Outlander's credit, I never felt pressured to spend any money in those first 30 hours, and had more materials than I needed. However, at a certain point, the roadblocks do start to pop up, especially as you unlock more gacha characters, and subsequently need to power them up. While you can continue playing Outlanders when those roadblocks hit, it's readily apparent that real money can "optimize" the experience. That becomes doubly true when you see the grind needed for unlocking special costumes or characters in events.

While I think Outlanders is overall one of the more generous gacha games I've played, there are nonetheless points where you will need to grind out activities to continue the story, or even wait a day until you can get more daily rewards. You consistently need to improve your Adventurer Rank, Ecological Level, and more to continue to the next main story quest. Whereas many Monster Hunter games start to open up after a few dozen hours, Outlanders feels like the opposite – a strong start that inevitably gets slowed down in monotony. I can also say I don't love spending nearly 20 percent of my time sifting through menus, and constantly tapping past screens to collect currencies. Again, that's an unfortunate nature of many gacha games, but Monster Hunter also inherently has a lot of its own menu surfing, meaning you're getting a double dose here.

items.title: The Mongoose Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
There’s a scene in the 1971 sci-fi cult classic where Charlton Heston’s helicopter is crash-landing, and just before the moment of impact it flies into an embankment just below the camera’s POV… where the craft’s explosion happens safely off-screen. It was a cheapo move in 1971 – they clearly didn’t really blow up the helicopter – and it’s a cheapo move in 2026, too, when Liam Neeson’s The Mongoose – now, somehow, playing at a multiplex near you! – pulls a similar stunt.

Sure, in The Mongoose the helicopter doesn’t even blow up off-camera, but that’s not the point (the crash-landing winds up being played for a laugh instead). What I’m talking about here is the threadbare sense that such a moment evokes for the viewer, the “a third of the budget of this movie must’ve gone to Liam Neeson” feeling that permeates the not-quite high-octane, not-quite thrilling picture.

And yet, there’s a likability factor wafting around this story, thanks largely to Neeson’s disarming “yeah, I taking a third of this film’s budget, and I’m gonna have fun doing it” affectation as he drives a stolen hotrod – do we still call them hotrods? – across various states while on the run from the police due to a crime he did not commit. Along for the ride, so to speak, are Ving Rhames, Marisa Tomei, and Michael Chiklis, all cashing in less than a third of the budget, presumably, but hitting their marks efficiently enough to get this thing over the finish line in a “Maybe just catch it on Prime Video eventually” kind of way.

The Mongoose tells its story through a mix of the chase Neeson’s Ryan “Fang” Flanagan is involved in and flashbacks to the former Special Forces soldier’s time in Afghanistan, specifically when he and his comrades (Rhames’ Tanker, Marcus Thomas’ Munch, and Ryan Morgan's Wiz) were captured by the enemy. Further flashbacks eventually fill in why Fang is on the run; specifically, his ex-wife Tara’s (Marisa Tomei) fiancé – “Todd something or other,” Fang growls – turns out to be not a nice person, and when Fang attempts to help Tara move out of the guy’s place, violence erupts. Next thing he knows, someone’s dead, and he’s stolen Todd something or other’s fancy, and quite fast, Ford Mustang. Other than that, all he’s got is a bullet in his leg, a vow to never be imprisoned again after his experience in the war, and the Mustang's built-in AI assistant, named Helene. “Is this, like, Siri?” Fang – and maybe Neeson too when he first read the script – asks.

Neeson's Fang is surprisingly chill about this situation, as he clearly has a death wish, having decided that he is not going to allow himself to be taken alive.

Helene, like many of the other characters (“characters”) in the episodic The Mongoose, serves as a foil for the surprisingly at-ease Fang to toss one-liners at while out-driving the various police who are pursuing him by land and air. Fang is surprisingly chill about this situation, as he clearly has a death wish, having decided that he is not going to allow himself to be taken alive. As the chase drags on, he eventually finds temporary refuge through the help of some other vets, and soon Fang begins to take on a legendary man-against-the-system status, thanks no doubt to his war hero cred, as well as the “live” CNN coverage of the high-speed pursuit, which IRL TV personality Laura Coates awkwardly hosts.

On the side of the law, there’s Maurice Marvel Meredith as Major James Tilton and Chiklis as Major Walter Pope. Suffice to say, one’s the good cop and one’s the bad copy, and never the twain shall meet, but also, never the twain shall have anything interesting or realistic to do or say. Rhames, unfortunately, seems to be struggling to deliver his lines at times, even while his very presence brings a sense of good will to the film. Tomei, meanwhile, is always likable, but most of her scenes are essentially just her on the phone with Neeson’s character, even as she miraculously overcomes some seriously life-changing events over the course of 24 hours or so.

As for the Mongoose of the title, it’s the beach in Mexico where Fang and Tara had their best days together, and as such it’s the ideal that Fang has fixated on – his “retirement” – if he somehow can escape his current, dire situation. But what he also must escape is the guilt of the men he left behind in Afghanistan, and it is this thread that director Mark Vanselow somehow scores with by the time the credits roll, aided no doubt by some keenly picked, and timed, needledrops, and a couple of very cleverly edited shots in the final moments of the film. The Mongoose may be working just one level above a direct-to-video cheapie for a lot of its running time, but it’s still got some heart, too.

items.title: Crimson Desert: Charting the Unknown Review So Far
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
Crimson Desert’s biggest strength is in the sheer volume of stuff it throws at you, allowing you to spend hundreds or even a thousand-plus hours doing everything from hunting animals with a bow to developing a gambling addiction at the tavern. So it’s not very surprising that Crimson Desert’s first paid DLC, called Charting the Unknown, prioritizes adding more on top of its already staggeringly large repertoire. So far, the interesting new activities that mostly focus on oceanic adventures are exactly as compelling as you’d hope, with ship-to-ship combat, underwater exploration, and romance options being among the list of new worthwhile features. On the other hand, existing activities that have added content, like the extra story missions, have mostly been uninspired retreads that don’t do anything to improve upon their established shortcomings. When Crimson Desert came out, I said that its content was a mile long and an inch deep, and for better or worse this DLC seems to say, “Here’s another half-mile.”

The most disappointing part of the DLC so far has been the additional story missions, which are only accessible once you’ve completed the base game’s already dense main story (a feat which only 10% of Steam players have done, judging by the achievements system). At least the handful of missions I’ve completed at this point have mostly served as an expanded epilogue of sorts, with Kliff fighting more difficult versions of old bosses from the existing story, and Damiane and Oongka fleshing out their less substantial stories as well.

I’m not far enough to know if any of these quests eventually become more interesting, but most of their objectives have been an oddly bland retracing of your steps, like going back to spend time with a familiar character and share a moment fishing together or arm wrestle someone to gather information as an apparent callback to an identical moment in the original story. I did get to a new stretch of the map just before getting distracted by the separate seafaring content, so hopefully this part of the DLC will pick up the pace, but so far it’s been about as unimpressive as I expected given the low bar for storytelling in Crimson Desert.

Much like the base content though, most of the effort seems to have been put into things that aren’t related to the story. Although most of my time has been spent dipping my toes into the water-based ship-crafting feature that’s the focus of this expansion, it feels like I’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg, with new resources to obtain, crewmates to hire, and even more activities to learn like harpooning fish and ship-to-ship combat before you can really begin your voyages properly.

It's going to take more time to fully engage with these new activities and judge whether or not they have the sea legs to keep me entertained for longer than a few hours, but at least right now I’m just impressed (yet again) by the fact that these systems exist in this adventure that’s already so damn packed with things to do. Gliding underwater on the back of a sea turtle and captaining your own pirate crew truly just feel completely bizarre in the context of Crimson Desert, and so far that’s been compelling enough to keep me moving forward even if some of the other added content isn’t great.

There’s still a ton I have to investigate, like additional base building and property management features, a challenging combat arena-style gauntlet, and my personal favorite – social links and romance mechanics for NPCs, which I’m very excited to check out once I’ve gotten my bearings (I’m just not ready to settle down yet, okay?!).

For all the stuff that’s been added, one thing that is the same since the last time I played is the number of bugs I’ve encountered in my brief time with the Charting the Unknown DLC. I’ve already had two hard crashes, one character wig out on me while I was trying to arm wrestle him (he was hilariously standing behind me during the match, arm bent unnaturally), and quite a few blurry or flickering textures that are impossible for me to not focus on during cutscenes. I’m still too early to tell if this is going to be a consistent issue, but in my time so far it’s been quite rocky from a technical perspective considering how much wonkiness I’ve encountered per hour played.

As expected with Crimson Desert, it’s going to take quite a bit of time to see and do enough to reach a definitive conclusion on Charting the Unknown, and I’m hopeful that the engaging and unexpected content that’s been added will be able to make up for some of the activities that feel like empty calories.

items.title: Ramayana: Rise of a Legend Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Hindi cinema has long looked to Hollywood as a benchmark for big-screen action; much of its 21st century style, for instance, wasinspired by Mission: Impossible 2. Ramayana: Rise of a Legend re-imagines the resplendent Hindu epic as a CGI-laden blockbuster at a time when the Marvel Cinematic Universe has become the de facto touchstone for big-budget adaptations. In that vein, Nitesh Tiwari’s undertaking does, in fact, resemble a Marvel movie. Unfortunately, that Marvel movie happens to be, a much-derided film whose floating head VFX had to be.

This resemblance takes hold in an early scene, in which the epic’s antagonist, Ravana (charismatic star Yash), prays atop a cliff to the creator-god Brahma, whose countenance takes the form of a disembodied constellation with an overly-expressive digital mouth. This excess fluidity is owed, in part, to the movie’s uncanny English dub, which was shown to press in the United States in lieu of the original Hindi version (which happens to be about 30 minutes longer than this 162-minute cut). Rather than traditional dubbing, the filmmakers developed their own in-house Generative A.I. technology (fittingly called Brahma A.I.) to sync up the characters’ lips to the flowery English dialogue. Some are calling it the future of cinema, but in its current incarnation, the result resembles exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches, à la.

This effect is befitting of such a robotic adaptation, one which briefly threatens to interrogate the several millennia-old text of the title (in the vein of recent Thai drama, which critiques the violence at the heart of national myths) before locking itself into a didactic approach. It’s a rigid depiction of both the subcontinent-spanning plot, as well as the theme of “Dharma,” or sacred duty, which the characters verbalize ad nauseum and follow unconditionally, and uninspiringly. For the uninitiated — which is to say, Sony’s target audience for the English dub, whose Indian subtitle (“Part 1”) has been slyly replaced with “Rise of a Legend” to convince people they’re paying for a complete story — the plot concerns an ongoing war between demigods the Devas and demons the Asuras.

The film re-imagines the villainous Ravana as a kind of liberator gone mad. The Asura leader begins by praying for the power to free his enslaved clan, and his island kingdom of Lanka, from Deva oppression before conquering nearby cities through violent conquest with his ambitious siblings by his side.. This forces the demigods to turn to the protector deity Vishnu, who re-incarnates himself as the human-born Rama (Ranbir Kapoor), one of four princes of the kingdom of Ayodhya. Prologues pile up on prologues for nearly an hour, as Rama grows up learning the ways of war and wisdom, since his divine destiny is to defeat the Asuras for good.

The filmmakers’ decision to cleave the story in half leaves it hanging in suspended animation.

However, the filmmakers’ decision to cleave the story in half leaves it hanging in suspended animation. It ends where the central plot of the Ramayana — Rama’s journey to rescuing his devoted wife Sita (Sai Pallavi) from Ravana’s clutches — finally kicks off in earnest, yielding an episodic experience where the central hero and villain are, at best, vaguely aware of one another’s existence. They never actually come into contact, leaving Ramayana: Rise of a Legend with the responsibility of establishing a protagonist and antagonist alluring enough that viewers with no pre-existing religious or cultural attachment will feel dutybound to return in one year’s time — or whenever the sequel is ready.

How does this work out? As far as Ravana is concerned, Kannada-language superstar Yash makes a meal of the character, imagined as an action anti-hero who dances in fiery worship of the destroyer god Shiva, and who nails his enemies with jackknife powerbombs, as vengeful gears turn slowly in his mind. Traditionally depicted with 10 heads side by side, the movie’s version of Ravana re-imagines this as a kind of fissure of personality, wherein 10 different versions of the demon king (some old, some young; some confident, some sniveling) converse and argue within his consciousness. He’s ruthless in one moment, but respectful in the next, making for the closest thing the movie has to complexity before it returns to the story’s binary good-versus-evil traditions. Add to this the fact that the movie’s Lanka is vibrant, energetic and sensual, compared to its stilted, austere Ayodhya, and it becomes hard to root for the ostensible “good guys.”

Unfortunately, this becomes doubly true whenever Rama is on screen. The film’s depiction of him is an utter bore. An embodiment of virtue in the abstract, the heroic prince — who agrees to live in exile for 14 years so one of his brothers can take the throne — is spoken of as a kind and capable figure, but his people’s worship of him is a default setting, rather than something earned through benevolence. After all, Rama is a central figure in Hinduism, so more than enough viewers will bring their own baggage to the movie. But as a story, it’s as rote as can be, a flaw that infects its dramatic DNA: Rama’s relationship to Sita. While Pallavi is afforded a tad more action and autonomy than most actresses in the role, the promise of a sword-wielding Sita is often cut short, returning her quickly to a two-dimensional damsel who shares little chemistry with her husband. Much like Kapoor’s Rama, Pallavi’s Sita is graceful in posture, but there’s little underlying either of them as actual human beings.

Rama, who lacks anything resembling outward opinions or an inner life beyond his Dharma, acquires weapons and knowledge not through practice or learning, but through gurus psychically unlocking these hidden abilities, as though the film were operating on video game logic. Each new chapter sees him “leveling up” as he fights a different, malformed CGI golem in a new forest setting, though at least he deserves credit for using his unlimited magical arrows to get these eyesores off our screens.

Saddled with clunky English dialogue, Kapoor is the perfect actor for this version of Rama, but that’s not the compliment it seems. His po-faced approach snaps perfectly into place, alongside a dramatically dull incarnation of the mythic hero, whose duty toward violent reprisal, and whose adoration by his legions of fans, is a given. Kapoor, a fourth generation Bollywood star, enjoys exactly such a quasi-religious fandom, even if the Hindu nationalist factions the film has been courting with its marketing (which refers to these myths as “history”) has since turned on him — a religious faux pas among Hindutva extremists.

Then again, with the movie’s attempts to stoke religious fervor being all but cancelled out, perhaps it makes sense to approach Ramayana: Rise of a Legend as a hermetically sealed experience, if only for a moment. This doesn’t do it any favors either; aesthetically, it’s a headache. While the grandeur of the costumes and archaic sets might draw one’s gaze in static moments, the cumulative effect of its many action scenes is often bewildering. Sure, some individual shots are big and bold in composition, but they’re frenetic and unfocused when strung together, with points of interest shifting in and out, left and right, and up and down at random. The fantasy fights lack the necessary physical and emotional weight to make a lasting impact, even before Rama’s fellow exiled brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey) delivers his umpteenth comic quip met by awkward dead air, adding to the Marvel-ness of it all.

Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman join hands for some booming compositions, but the music — much of which has been trimmed for the shorter cut, which features little singing or dancing — is tasked with scoring scenes and set pieces with no rhythm of their own. The film feels entirely off-kilter even before characters open their distracting, digitally-rendered mouths. That some of them sound like whiny, posh South Bombay youngsters is, perhaps, something only viewers who’ve spent time in India might really notice in the English version, but it nonetheless robs the dialogue-heavy drama of its potential grandeur.

There are fleeting pluses to be found throughout the runtime. The movie, for instance, features one moment of evocative suggestion — a harsh cut from a nightmarish vision to an empty throne, denoting the weight of Rama’s regal responsibility — but anything resembling moral dilemma is quickly swallowed by prescriptive plot developments, which leave little room for meaningful character arcs or emotional possibility. A climactic mid-air battle does, quite mercifully, manage to capture the imagination without much haphazard distraction. However, this scene doesn’t actually involve Rama at all. Its focus, instead, is a supporting character barely glimpsed up until that point, leaving Kapoor’s dreary protagonist to promise a more cogent narrative in the sequel.

The duology’s success is all but guaranteed in India and among its diaspora, given how deeply entrenched the Ramayana remains in Hindu and Indian culture (its release coincides with the major festival Diwali). However, to anyone not already attuned to the tale, it’s hard to imagine this version being a meaningful enough introduction to bring novice viewers back. It has neither the emotional hook nor the soul to compensate for its lack of visual momentum, and its reliance on a half-baked tech to appeal to a wider audience impedes what little drama exists at its core.

items.title: Yaga Episode 3 Recap and Review
items.author: Jessie Wade
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Season 1, Episode 3. Episodes 1-3 are now streaming on AMC+ in the US and Crave in Canada, with new episodes releasing on Fridays at midnight PT.

Yaga Episode 3 wastes no time diving right back into this eerie, witchy tale, while answering some of our biggest questions after last week’s debut.

We pick up right where Episode 2’s cliffhanger left off – on the beach with Logan’s body – prior to getting confirmation from the police that, yes, it is in fact Logan’s lifeless body (not Henry’s) and that blood was found near a window open in his bedroom. There’s a moment of confusion for the viewer as Rapp sees Logan’s eyes jump open, and we see that they are ice blue – like Henry’s.

By now, we know Rapp has been hallucinating more frequently and this is possibly either from the drugs from the night before (because he honestly looks like he’s still high) or something dark and ominous that’s happening to him.

We see a pattern in relation to “time” in Yaga. This is confirmed when Carson recounts what happened the previous night at Henry’s party where we learn that “a few hours” had passed between seeing Logan disappear into his room upstairs, and Carson finding Rapp on the beach. Originally, it seemed like time had passed, but nothing substantial.

As we continue on with more unexplained moments in this story, Rapp tries to put a move on Carson in his hotel room, which she rejects. He then goes to lie down on his bed and falls asleep almost too quickly – Carson comes and kneels down next to the bed and we see the clock turn to 3:33 (not the first time we’ve seen this either), while intense, whispering voices begin to take over as she leans in to almost kiss him. Rapp gently opens his eyes and sees Pam, Henry’s ex-girlfriend, seductively pulling a white feather out of his mouth.

He suddenly jolts out of his actual sleep and awakens some time later in the day. We also notice a small circle tattoo on Carson’s wrist before they head over to forensics, which seems to be placed in the shot intentionally for us to refer back to later…

Going to the mortuary, we see Logan’s corpse – well, most of it. In the episode’s biggest WTF moment, we learn Logan’s penis was severed from his body and he was castrated. It turns out he was also stabbed with an ancient knife made out of Obsidian and human bone – which Katherine later classifies as an Aztec ceremonial midwife sacrificial knife, connected to deities with symbols representing sexual desire and fertility. All signs so far point to Logan being murdered, and Carson and the police on staff are searching for more evidence, especially as this new case potentially relates to Henry.

We see Carson walk up to a small church to meet Logan’s mom, Alice (played by Sarah Strange). The dark, moody shots and heavy music come together to create an emotionally beautiful scene of grief between the two women. They sit on a bench in the cemetery together and more is revealed about Logan that we hadn’t known before. That includes Logan changing his hair and working out constantly – like he was trying to become Henry himself, perhaps.

Alice reveals her hate for the Parks and shares how she heard a rumor that Logan and Henry bought one of Pam’s lame hens from her and joked they were going to sacrifice it. She then explains passionately how she could see everything affecting Logan, saying, “Everyday, I’d see that growing in him. That thing getting bigger and thicker and darker and pulling him further and further away from God, and closer and closer to the Devil.” Carson asks about Logan’s dad, but Alice dismisses the questions.

While Carson is with Alice, we see Rapp jogging on the beach. Pam happens to be running in front of him. He tries to catch up to her and, as he does, she all of a sudden splits into three versions of herself, distorted in Rapp’s view. She calls his name and he trips over a log, seeing more visions and a sinister mask staring back at him, as he peers up at Pam who is somehow immediately next to him with a cheeky comment.

Before Carson and Rapp decide to head back over to Henry’s house to check for more leads, Carson inquires if Henry and Logan were possibly in a relationship, giving Rapp unintentional fuel to speculate on Carson’s sexuality as well, which she avoids divulging.

"The Maiden, the Mother, and the Crone."

As the duo begin surveying Logan’s room, you can see the pile of bloodied sheets next to the window, and they begin slowly uncovering more and more clues as they go along. Interestingly, they find drug powder in a canister with the same triangle symbol we saw from the previous episodes – a symbol known as the – which has multiple interpretations. In Celtic mythology it is said to represent sacred femininity and the Triple Goddess archetype: the Maiden, the Mother, and the Crone. Baba Yaga in Slavic folklore is known as the “Crone,” so we’ll have to wait and see how that relates (if at all) as the series continues.

Carson and Rapp also notice the chicken foot hanging from Logan’s lampshade, previously in Henry’s room – and we can now pretty safely assume it’s from the chicken he and Henry were rumored to have sacrificed.

Just when they are trying to figure out how Logan disappeared from his room the night before, Rapp discovers the bookshelf is actually a secret door into another room… a small, eerie spot illuminated by red lights, despite the rest of the house having no power. A desk with a tape recorder and an archive of dozens upon dozens of cassette tapes are stacked on shelves.

As they dig in further, Carson and Rapp find out there’s a recording from the previous night in Henry’s bedroom – from when Logan was having sex with the woman wearing the angel wings. We hear Logan demanding to be called “Henry,” making us wonder if Henry was even at the party last night – despite his phone being traced to that location.

Rapp searches through Henry’s room, discovering – disturbingly – a wired bug hidden on his nightstand, which is triggered to record in Logan’s “secret office” whenever someone speaks in the room. Carson plays more of the recording from the prior night and they discover Pam is the one who was having sex with Logan, just hours before his death – making her officially a suspect in Logan’s murder.

As we’re processing that surge of information, Rapp’s eyes suddenly catch on a drop of blood on the floor next to the bed – he drops down and peers under, seeing something bloody smeared on the floor. He quickly pulls the bed back, pushing it out of the way, and as Carson comes into the room we see the Triskelion symbol drawn wide across the floor in blood, with three white chicken feathers near each point in the symbol – seemingly signifying a curse or some kind of spell. It’s even more eerie with the haunting music, which pulls you into its claws and feels like a spell wrapping itself tightly around you, right as Baba Yaga narrates through the end of the episode.

We see solid character development in this episode, with Clark Backo stepping more into her role as Carson and raising the question of where her boundary lies between professionalism and intrigue. Noah Reid as Rapp brings more grit to his role and shows a darker, more intense side to his character – I’m looking forward to seeing how both of these characters expand into this world from here.

Some lingering questions we now have going into Episode 4: Do Henry and Logan have the same dad and is that why Alice despises the Parks so much? Is Pam a witch or maybe Baba Yaga in disguise? Did Logan put the spell under Henry’s bed, and if so, why and who’s really behind it?

items.title: Nocturne Episodes 1 & 2 Recap and Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Episodes 1 and 2, which are available on Apple TV now.

Apple TV’s new thriller series, Nocturne, aims to draw audiences in with just the right balance of the familiar and the unexpected. The show asks what happens when a boy thought to be the victim of a serial killer returns alive, and follows the criminal mastermind as he maneuvers law enforcement during their race to save any other victims who may still be out there. Over the course of these first two episodes, viewers are left with questions — a mix of plot-driven intrigue, interest in character development, and a touch of side-eye around potential logic gaps or plot conveniences.

Nocturne is based on Lars Kepler’s crime novels (The Sandman and Lazarus), and adapted by Rowan Joffe and John Hlavin for TV. These debut episodes lay the groundwork for convicted killer Jurek Walter’s unfolding scheme to free himself (he is astonishingly well played by Stephen Graham), set against multiple law enforcement officers’ attempts to a) stop him from doing more harm and b) find any of the still-living victims. Jurek was convicted of a series of brutal killings, which devastated a small town. He managed to get a jury to buy into an insanity defense, or we must presume he did, as he’s in a psychiatric hospital rather than a prison. (Side note: how he pulled that off is a nagging question, as nothing in his demeanor suggests an insanity defense would fly… If it’s simply that he’s a sociopath, wouldn’t that apply to all killers? Moving on.)

From a technical perspective, the show does a beautiful job of dropping us in this world. The opening shot of Episode 1, “Lazarus, Come Forth,” establishes a sense of foreboding, danger, and claustrophobia that will become a refrain throughout the series. We get the sense that the creature we are encountering is not unlike a lion in a cage. The camera moves down a cold, concrete hallway toward cells that feel (purposefully) hidden and forgotten — the shot is all the more suffocating because the dark walls of the cell entryways initially obscure the sides of the frame. This is our introduction to Jurek, and it’s notable that the series starts by putting us in the mindset of the killer. He feels trapped and eager to get out. For some yet-to-be-revealed purpose, his gritty, simultaneously menacing and soothing voice whispers to the patient next door, luring the man to seek freedom by any means necessary, even with violence (in this case, against himself). This is Jurek’s central arc across the first two episodes.

He is brilliant and adept at psychological warfare. He also seems to believe he’s entitled to his freedom, or at the very least that there is some legal loophole that will get his conviction overturned if only he can expose the lie that former homicide detective Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber) told to seal Jurek’s fate. Jurek taunts Jonah towards the close of the first episode with an offer of “the truth for the truth” when Jonah and Special Agent Quinn (Poorna Jagannathan, lately of Lanterns) visit him. In other words, Jurek will help them find more of his victims, specifically Felicia Frost — the missing sister of Michael, the boy who’s come back from the dead — if Jonah confesses to lying in court. This raises the stakes for everyone, including Agent Quinn, who’s already taken a risk by bringing a retired cop she doesn’t know this close to her case. If his old lie blows it up, that’s on her, with a missing girl’s life on the line.

While some crime dramas give us only as much information as the characters searching for answers have, this one puts the audience a step ahead. It’s an interesting choice, and may ultimately be a misdirect.

While some crime dramas give the audience only as much information as the characters searching for answers have, this one puts the audience a step ahead. It’s an interesting choice, and may ultimately be a misdirect. Here’s what appears to have happened: a hospital worker named Karl (Rory Culkin) is assigned to the team that oversees Jurek. Their first encounter, like others in the series, is crafted with impressive tension: Karl searches for a missing weapon beneath Jurek’s metal bed, gets caught by his pant leg, and can’t free himself before Jurek comes to from a sedative — the trapped animal motif plays throughout. Before the scene is over, Jurek has pressed a note into Karl’s pocket, urging him to smuggle it out to his lawyer (more on the questions this raises in a bit).

The note Jurek hands Karl seems to set everything in motion: the strong implication is that, lawyer or no lawyer, it contained Jurek’s instruction to an accomplice to free Michael. Jonah is actively drawn back into the case when Michael turns up alive, as the children’s mother, Ida Frost (Chrissy Metz), and the residents of the town trust him more than anyone else in law enforcement. Also advocating for his participation is FBI agent Saga Bauer (Zazie Beetz), his goddaughter, the child of his deceased partner, and someone he effectively raised. (She eventually goes undercover as a patient in Jurek’s secured ward in order to ascertain who is leaking messages and endangering lives.)

The reality is, Jonah has clearly never given up on finding the remaining missing persons associated with the case: as Agent Bauer discovers via his giant murder board, he’s been methodically searching an enormous grid, single-handedly, for years. The case is deeply personal for both of them. Jonah carries guilt for having quit the force after the (seemingly unrelated?) accidental death of his wife and child. And Jurek (or rather his accomplice) was responsible for kidnapping Bauer’s stepmother, Rebecca. It’s also implied that Bauer’s father committed suicide after his wife’s disappearance. Through Agent Quinn’s vocal skepticism, the show addresses the inappropriateness of having either Jonah or Bauer involved in the investigation, given their personal connections to Jurek. The story excuses the conflict of interest (not to mention that Jonah is no longer an officer of the law) by pointing to their familiarity with the case and the ticking clock on saving Felicia. The dynamics and interwoven tragedies all tied to Jurek stretch credulity, but the production value and strength of the performances are enough to keep the viewer engaged through a good deal of character, plot, and relationship table-setting. At its core, this is a battle of three savants with real stakes: two on the victims’ side, deploying their individual skills to best a mysterious, murderous genius. That brings us to the tightrope the series walks.

When crime dramas lean on preternatural intellect, whether it’s Sherlock Holmes or his foil, Moriarty, they run the risk of reading as a lazy sort of magic trick, where the detective or killer effortlessly “knows things” they’d need to in order to keep the story moving. Indeed, Jonah’s near-instant recognition of where Michael was being held, and Jurek’s Derren Brown-level ability to read people (pegging Karl’s guitar playing and Jonah’s partner’s violent alcoholism), open the door to the kind of conveniences that could lose a modern audience as the series unfolds. It already causes one to wonder: if Jurek is in possession of that kind of mental acuity, why did he get caught while his partner went free? Fortunately, Graham, who stunned the world with Adolescence last year, is deeply compelling, allowing us to give ourselves over to his performance.

That isn’t to undercut the potent talent of the rest of the cast, or the visual storytelling. The show is beautifully shot, with well-crafted production design.
