It immerses us in a rustic exterior world that vacillates between gray and worn, and comfortingly familiar. The forest landscapes are striking, but dense and dangerous in a way that mirrors the cold, stifling confines of the hospital Jurek is housed in.

Schreiber is delivering a grounded, understated portrayal of a grieving man who is just a bit too tired to fully fight against terrible ideas (Bauer’s undercover operation) and far too invested to stop himself from digging, with or without permission. One moment that stands out is when Agent Quinn tells Jonah she’s sorry for the loss of his wife and child; he nods, and unbearable pain flashes in his eyes for an instant before he moves on. Beetz is convincing and deeply affecting as a chameleon-like agent willing to harm herself (physically or otherwise) to close a case. It’s clear that this particular operation may drive her to a breaking point for multiple reasons: Jurek’s uncanny ability to read others and play on their weaknesses, her own stepmother’s disappearance (which he is connected to), and, not least of all, that it taps into the trauma of a woman who was the child of a mentally ill mother and addict father. That fear comes through as she prepares to enter the ward, right after visiting her mother. Beetz gives the sense that Bauer is unsure whether she’s crossing a line she won’t be able to come back from, where fact and fiction are too close. Bill Camp is also endearing as Chief Ellison, particularly as he talks about what the Frost kids meant to the town; he looks vulnerable, like a man who knows he is out over his skis, but wishes he wasn’t.

It took a moment for me to recognize Culkin as the compassionate nurse, Karl. Physically, his hair is doing a great deal to support the transformation, but this is also a side of the actor less seen on screen. There was one moment, when he first sees Jurek on the security cameras, in which I was left to wonder if he had some nefarious intent. But for the most part, he reads as a man of incredible kindness and skill with patients whom most of society writes off and exiles. That said, it’s odd that an employee who demonstrates an extraordinary amount of empathy is tapped for a job that puts him right in the crosshairs of a person known to exploit those instincts, and in a dangerous environment that requires a certain degree of toughness. Additionally, Karl, who is clearly driven by financial need (he accepts the new job the moment he’s informed that it comes with a raise and tells Jurek he can’t afford to lose it), inexplicably risks his career for a dangerous criminal he just met.

So, that leaves us with a couple of options: this is a piece of plotting that doesn’t logically track, or Karl isn’t who we think he is. If it’s the latter, perhaps Karl was “sent” into the hospital with purpose. It’s strangely convenient that Jurek’s day nurse went missing (and is likely dead), making room for Karl to take over. Theoretically, the patient who injures himself in the opening sequence could have gotten word to Jurek’s partner to get rid of the day nurse and make room for Karl. But how could Jurek have known that the exact right personality type for his purposes was working a few floors above him, let alone that he’d get the job? Was Karl a plant, then, and Jurek’s accomplice? That doesn’t square with their first encounter, where, with no witnesses, Jurek treats Karl as a stranger and insists he is still a human deserving care. And if someone else on staff was steering Karl, Jurek already has a partner on the inside, so why would he need Karl? Those are just a few of the questions that may or may not pay off at the close of the series. There are smaller dangling threads as well. For example, Jonah finds footprints both in the building where Michael was held and outside the missing day nurse’s home, so why in the world would he hold them back from the FBI? Ostensibly, he’d do anything to find Felicia, so that type of behavior simply doesn’t track. Ironically, the serial killer is doing a better job of asking for help and relying on a partner.

That said, the series works in no small part because Graham is simply impossible to look away from. He’s playing a killer who appears to have a (forgive the reference) code that makes sense to him. He says he “wants people to pay for their crimes.” Yes, that was in reference to Jonah’s “lie,” but the way he looks at the nurse who is rude to Karl reminds me of Hannibal Lecter’s deep disdain for bad manners. Graham’s depiction of Jurek is utterly magnetic and mercurial; when Jonah and Quinn visit, he breaks into a fit of giggles at the idea that she’s a “special” agent, as if the word itself is a joke, and moments later he’s commanding the room, telling them with understated menace that they’re only there because he brought them there. He really does seem to own them. The minute he’s off the screen, I crave more time with him.

This entirely serves the series, because it allows us to believe that others could fall under his spell, even Bauer, a smart, capable, stony FBI agent with oceans to lose. There is a deep irony that he’s maneuvering and clawing his way to freedom, given his brutal kill method of burying victims alive. He complains that he’s been in solitary, but his partner has kept a child in the dark so long that the boy went temporarily blind. There’s also a very small possibility that he is, in some way, innocent, and that he has been “made worse” by his circumstances. Either way, for those on both sides of the law, this is a story about freedom, loss, redemption, and revenge, and the first two episodes have given me enough to stick with it for now.

items.title: Avatar: Seven Havens Season 1 Finale Review and Recap
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
One thing that’s abundantly clear in the final four episodes of Avatar: Seven Havens “Book 1: Survival” is that between all the mysteries, theorizing, and big plot questions – how are there two Avatars? What did Korra do to cause the Cataclysm? What happened to Pavi (Saheli Khan) and Nisha’s (Aishu Devan) parents? – the far more important question is, and has always been, how this will impact the relationship between the twins? And to answer that, the finale is a heartbreaker, featuring one of the darkest, most upsetting endings in the Avatar franchise, while still somehow providing hope, heart, and above all, humor.

That’s a lot to tackle, and to be clear we do still get movement on the overarching mysteries of the series that should take us all the way through Book 4. That includes the reveal of what’s needed to heal the world… While fans guessed what was going on, and there is likely much more to come, it turns out that the Seven Chakras that coincide with Seven Havens are directly tied to Pavi. Specifically, as the Faceless Queen Agam (Sakina Jaffrey) discovers during a spiritual alignment in Episode 11, “Battle of the Ruins,” Pavi’s chakras are all messed up. And once she’s able to face her fear of being revealed as the Avatar in the finale, “The Root Chakra,” she unlocks – guess what – her Root Chakra.

Both we, the audience, and Nisha are surprised that it’s Pavi who can unlock these alone; it was completely reasonable to speculate that the only way of stopping the fear literally bubbling under the Haven of Ellora was through Nisha and Pavi working together. Instead, the additional shocker is that somehow Nisha summoned that fear, killing her and Pavi’s parents in the process. Pavi was protected from the resulting rock slide by some sort of green energy, which took her leg… And Nisha, while able to hold back an energy dome about to consume the Haven in Episode 12, “The Dome,” is nowhere near as strong as Pavi, who single-handedly dispels the fear and begins to reconnect with past Avatars, as well as charting her path to her next destination, The Floating Isles (or Wilds – there are no closed captions on the screeners provided by Paramount).

(Side-note: there’s a ton of lore we could get into here, but we’ll save it for the section below.)

But in between all that, these episodes are really about two things: Pavi and Nisha, and how we react to fear. On the former, the show has managed to craft a powerful sisterly bond over the course of 13 episodes that feels real… Pavi is gutted by the revelation that Nisha killed their parents, but she’s far more upset that Nisha lied to her about it. And we’re left in a place where Pavi is finally owning up to her destiny, but seems harsher and more closed off (despite unlocking the Chakra) than the goofy weirdo who befriended rocks and bugs in the initial episodes. Meanwhile, Nisha is being cheered by the crowd in Ellora at the end, a flip on the fear of the Avatar that dogged her every move. But she’s just seen Pavi display more power than she ever has, and that clearly alarms her. They haven’t exactly changed positions, but it’s clear this resolution isn’t as simple as “hooray, fear cured!”

That gets to the second part, which we’ve been harping on all season: fear. The show hasn’t necessarily been subtle about how it’s reflecting our current world (or at least the world of several years ago when they were writing, developing, and animating this), but when a character says “We can’t just hide from this scary bubble” or “Freedom of choice is all I’ve ever wanted” they’re basically putting it out there what metaphorical levels the show is working on. And what works about it is that the series still functions as a rollicking adventure show and a sweet all-ages animated show while still being very blunt about where it leans politically.

And that’s what the best of entertainment should be doing, right? Commenting on our real world while also working as, you know, entertainment. Seven Havens has absolutely nailed that balance over 13 episodes. Not only that, but these final four address a number of fan “concerns” that have bubbled up. One of them has been about the “weak” bending, which one could venture comes from the fact that bending is disappearing from the world (as stated multiple times) and which we now know at least in part comes from these seven Chakras being blocked. But also, Pavi taking on the fear energy dome in the finale . No pun intended on earthbending, but saving up your big bending stunts for the finale makes sense in terms of the build of a season.

The show hasn’t necessarily been subtle about how it’s reflecting our current world.

The other question about the show has been why Pavi and Nisha are nine years old, with concerns raised that they’re trying to age down the Avatar series even further than has already happened. While one could point out here that it’s a children’s cartoon on Nickelodeon, and apologies this isn’t catering to you, an adult who watched the original series 20 years ago, this finale cemented that not only is this show going crazy dark and upsetting – with Pavi and Nisha’s parents abandoning Nisha, then dying in a rockslide – but at the very least Pavi is starting to grow up by the end of the episode. Her hair is different, and Khan does a masterful job of maturing her voice. There’s been speculation about a time jump going into further seasons, and given the epic journey nature of the show (as also set up in the finale) that seems likely… They won’t be nine forever.

Okay, before we get too much farther, let’s recap the specific episodes (briefly), though they all work nicely together as a four-part finale. First up is Episode 10, “Ghosts and Spirits.” The thrust here is that Chancellor Kayoko (Jennifer Sun Bell) has been driven mad by the fear anomaly, and has the whole city under martial law. While Pavi deals with the metaphorical ghosts of her parents after discovering her childhood home, Nisha encounters the first spirit we’ve seen on the show, which leads her to the place we later discover she freaked out at and killed her parents. And in the midst of this, Agam discovers the duo and leads them to her hideout.

Then in Episode 11, “Battle of the Ruins,” Kayoko makes the exceedingly poor decision to redirect the bubbling pit of fear energy under Ellora to the hideout of the Faceless. We also discover definitively that Jae (Major Curda) never betrayed the Order of the White Lotus; he was just trying to not get arrested so he can free them later. We also get info on the Chakras from Agam, and they end up fighting the bubbling fear energy together, barely escaping in time.

Episode 12, “The Dome,” heads back to Ellora as Nisha solo tries to stop the energy, now in the form of (yep) a dome, while Pavi holds it back. Kayoko isn’t having any of it, and breaks Nisha’s hold, releasing the dome, which consumes our twins… Leading to a vision of their mother. Also, Jae and his boyfriend Datu (Topher Ngo) break up, which is a real bummer for ‘shippers but lets Jae be free to travel in the next episode.

And then we’ve got the finale, Episode 13, “The Root Chakra,” which we’ve covered a chunk of already. To touch on a few other points/where we leave folks, Pavi leaves for the next Haven with Jae by her side, while Nisha stays in Ellora with Karthik (Akshay Khanna). Kayoko is still possessed by the fear entity, which seems… interesting. Agam, meanwhile, seems to stay in Ellora, while she names Zi (Dianne Doan) the Faceless Queen, and the rest of the Faceless presumably head to Republic Forest, as planned.

If this first, excellent season is any indication, Books 2, 3, and 4 will all do what Book 1 did so well: lead with its heart on its sleeve.

So, lots more to explore when we get into Book 2, particularly with the twins separated and on very different paths. We still don’t know why or how there are two Avatars, what led to Nisha’s parents wanting to abandon her, how Korra caused the Cataclysm, or why Pavi’s Chakras are blocked. But if this first, excellent season is any indication, Books 2, 3, and 4 will all do what Book 1 did so well: lead with its heart on its sleeve.

Avatar Easter Eggs, References, and Connections

Before we get to the Easter eggs and references, it’s important to recognize the untimely, awful passing of voice actor Eric Bauza at age 46 on October 25. While Bauza didn’t voice any of the main roles on the series, he was, as always, a utility player. In these final four episodes alone he’s credited with Jin-Woo, Townsperson, Elloran Citizens, Kosal, Pich, Faceless, Faceless Bandits, Faceless Kids, Firebender, Guard #2, Benders, Guards, and Ellorans – just to give you an idea of how important this legend was to the series. And not only that, but he also stood out as Pudding Guy in the previous chunk of episodes, a delightful addition that seemed to be the heir to The Last Airbender’s Cabbage Merchant. What they’ll do with that role in subsequent seasons is TBD, but Bauza leaves a gap in the world of Avatar that can’t readily be filled.

Not to make an abrupt turn, but let’s talk about those blocked chakras. This was first introduced in The Last Airbender and explored when Aang was injured by Azula, and was unable to access the Avatar State. Here, while Pavi goes HAM on that red energy dome in the finale, she does enter the Avatar State at all, likely because her Chakras are blocked. But we do get a strange red glow around her, and that greenish glow that protected her from Nisha’s rock slide in the flashback, which seems to be something new.

Speaking of something new, when Pavi does finally unlock her Root Chakra, she sees constellation versions of the previous Avatars Kyoshi, Roku, Aang, and finally Korra (aka, the four Avatars before Pavi and Nisha). Without getting too deep in the weeds here, at the end of Legend of Korra, thanks to a big fight between Raava and Vaatu, the spirits of order and chaos, Korra’s connection to the Avatar Cycle was severed, then begun anew. So whatever Pavi is seeing in this Rainbow Road/constellation deal is something different (or, since Korra went on many adventures after the final season of Legend of Korra, perhaps she experienced something different first).

As for Easter eggs, these episodes are remarkably light by comparison to the rest of the season, but we do have a few. Jae proudly declares “I will always be Team Avatar” in Episode 11, giving us our first glimpse of this show’s, well, Team Avatar – something we’ve gotten in both The Last Airbender and The Legend of Korra.

In Episode 12, Pavi makes an absolutely ridiculous mud mask for Nisha to disguise her – which works, as an Elloran refers to her as “old man.” This is just part of a long tradition of Team Avatar having the absolute worst disguises that, somehow, beyond all reason, always actually disguise them.

And one blink and you’ll miss it Easter egg, as everyone flees the energy dome in Ellora at the beginning of Episode 13, sees a citizen quickly walk in front of the camera holding – what else – an armful of cabbages.

items.title: South Park Season 29, Episode 4 Review: 'Guinea Pig on a Stick'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
This season of South America started off well enough, but there's been a real struggle to build any real momentum over the long haul. It often feels like the writers aren't sure whether to fully commit to the idea of doing more classical standalone episodes this year or try to build an overarching narrative. And so we're left with a season that constantly reminds us that "November is coming," without anything more insightful to add than the constant allusions to Grand Theft Auto 6.

To its credit, Episode 4 tries to build on the foundation of the previous chapters and establish a more coherent conflict for the embattled South America. This time around, rising beef prices and high demand have robbed South America Elementary of its precious sloppy joes. It falls on Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and yes, Little Randy, to save the day and find a solution to the town's woes.

The results of these efforts are mixed, at best. The South American beef storyline relies a little too much on hitting the same gags over and over again. Seeing rich snobs devour South American beef and promptly explode in a shower of buttery diarrhea is funny the first couple of times, but it gets old pretty quickly without any real escalation. The same goes for the constant "South American beef" wordplay. I will say, though, that I got a big kick out of the heated steakhouse rivalry and the conflict between Ruth's Chris, Sizzler, and Texas Roadhouse. The same goes for the prolonged dig at rich, suburban wannabe cowboys.

Again, I just wish all of this built to something a little more memorable, coherent, and politically insightful. It feels like there's so much worth lampooning in American politics right now, and yet the series is being oddly subdued and wishy-washy. After such a Trump-heavy Season 27 and 28, it seems like Trey Parker, Matt Stone, and their team are loath to return to that well. And so, despite the fact that we're literally one week away from the midterm elections in the U.S., South Park has oddly little to say on that front. Maybe it would have been better if the series waited a little longer before coming back.

What South Park does have right now, though, is Little Randy. I was hoping that particular twist from Episode 3 would carry over, and boy does it. It's a lot of fun seeing Randy embrace his new role as a beer-chugging fourth grader, and in watching Stan deal with the constant embarrassment of having his father hanging around. Amusingly enough, he's the only one who seems to actually resent Little Randy's presence.

I especially enjoyed Randy's attempts to cement his new status in the friend group, crowning them "Goonies" and referring to Cartman as "Chunk." Cartman's line, "Why does your dad keep talking about gooning?" is easily the highlight of the entire episode. As much as the series may be struggling on the political and topical humor front right now, there's a lot of potential to mine with Randy's latest little crusade. Hopefully these next two episodes can take full advantage of that potential.

items.title: The iPhone 18 Pro Max Takes an Incredible Design and Just Makes It Faster
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
Every year there’s a new iPhone, and while the iPhone Duo is a huge departure from what Apple has done in the past, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is nearly identical to last year’s model. Apple didn’t do much to drastically change the Pro Max, but instead tweaked some things under the phone to make it a bit more useful.

The most obvious improvement is the A20 Pro, which is significantly stronger than the A19 Pro in last year’s phone. But the most useful improvement has been to Siri. The improvements Apple has made to its ‘Apple Intelligence’ has made Siri more useful than it has been since the company first tried revamping the assistant with AI back in 2024.

So, if you’ve already upgraded to the iPhone 17 Pro last year, there isn’t much reason to upgrade again. But if you’ve been on the fence and need an upgrade, you could really do a lot worse than the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

When I say that the iPhone 18 Pro Max looks just like the iPhone 17 Pro Max, I mean it. Even if I put the two phones on a table next to each other, you’d be hard-pressed to figure out which is which. They both measure 0.34 inches thick, even though the 18 Pro Max is a bit heavier, at 8.78 ounces, compared to the 17's 8.22 ounces. The only way I can tell my iPhone 17 Pro Max from the iPhone 18 Pro Max is that the Pro Max Apple sent me for review has the new Black colorway.

But while the phone’s chassis being unchanged might sound like a bad thing, it really is a case of not fixing something that’s not broken. The best part of the iPhone 17 Pro Max was its camera shelf, which virtually eliminates the phone wobbling when it’s put down on a table. For some reason, other phone manufacturers really haven’t adopted this design language yet, but I’ll just say every time I use an Android device lately, I miss the camera shelf, however absurd that may sound.

The rest of the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s layout is also unchanged. On the right side of the phone, you still get the power/lock button, along with the capacitive Camera Control Button. And just like on the 17 Pro Max, the camera button is extremely easy to hit on accident, so be mindful of it.

Over on the left side is the volume rocker and the Action Button, which I have set to enable or disable Do Not Disturb mode. You can go into the settings and swap it to one of 12 different actions, or just disable it entirely. But I like to keep it on DnD, so that I can make my phone stop blowing up when I’m overwhelmed.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max’s display is also unchanged, at 2868 x 1320, and with a gorgeous OLED panel. Everything I watch or play on the phone looks incredible, with absolutely vibrant colors. It’s also rated for up to 3,000 nits of brightness, which means it gets bright enough to use outside comfortably. The only other phone I’ve used that comes close is the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, but that shouldn’t be too surprising, given that Samsung manufactures a lot of Apple’s displays.

Apple has also shrunk the Dynamic Island on the display, so you have less of the display area blacked out at the top of the display. It is still there, and it’s still visible, but I don’t really notice the difference until I have the 18 Pro and the 17 Pro next to each other. There have been phones that have eliminated the need for a camera cutout, and the iPhone still isn’t there, but hopefully by shrinking it, Apple is getting closer to getting rid of it altogether.

I have had some problems with Siri for a few years now. For some reason, around 2022 or 2023, Apple's voice assistant stopped working for me most of the time I tried to use it. And it's not like I'm constantly trying to talk to the little robot in my phone or anything, but it got so bad that I couldn't even yell at my phone to skip a song on Apple Music reliably when I was in the shower.

But with the improvements to Apple Intelligence in iOS 27, Siri has dramatically improved. I am no longer asking it to set a timer, only to have it hang and then ask me if I want to query ChatGPT. It just sets the damn timer. I don't want to give Apple too many roses for this, because in a lot of ways, Siri has simply regained functionality that it had a decade ago.

Of course, Apple has also worked in a bunch of AI features, as well, which will let Siri scan through your messages or photos to help you plan events or find information. And, I'm sure that's useful for a lot of people, and it does appear to work well, but I'm old and too used to doing everything manually, and even this new version of 'Apple Intelligence' hasn't converted me to automating everything I do on my phone.

For the most part, the camera system in the iPhone 18 Pro Max is exactly the same as the iPhone 17 Pro Max, with the only real difference being the addition of a variable aperture. The aperture on the 18 Pro works just like it does on a regular camera, with a mechanical shutter that widens or narrows to control the amount of light in the shot.

For most people, this probably won’t make much of a difference, and the auto aperture setting is going to work fine. However, if you like to have more control of your photos, Apple has added ‘Pro controls’ to the camera app, that lets you dial in the aperture for your shot. It works extremely well, but I still don’t think I’m going to abandon my DSLR and rely on the iPhone cameras. Though, it should come in handy at events like CES, where I typically need to take photos on my phone in the interest of time.

The camera itself is still great, though, and photos look great without really needing to spend a lot of time finding the perfect shot. It’s just nice that Apple has added some finer control for anyone that wants it.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is powered by the A20 Pro, along with 12GB of RAM, and it is surprising just how much performance Apple was able to squeeze out of it. In every test I’ve run on the new Pro, it far surpasses its predecessor.

In GeekBench 7, the iPhone 18 Pro Max gets a single-core score of 3867 points and a multi-core score of 11,204 points, compared to the 17 Pro, which gets 2,865 and 7,120 points, respectively. That’s a massive 44% improvement to multi-core performance, and a 29% improvement to single-core performance.

Even compared to the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra the iPhone 18 Pro Max is 24% faster, with the Android device getting 2,725 points for single-core and 8,786 points for multi-core.

When it comes to gaming, the GPU stapled to the A20 Pro is also impressive, with the 18 Pro scoring 8001 points in the Wild Life Extreme test, compared to 4795 from the 17 Pro Max and 5758 points from the Galaxy S26 Ultra. That makes the 18 Pro Max 33% faster than Samsung’s 2026 flagship.

Just like the 17 Pro, the 18 Pro Max is cooled by a vapor chamber, and it's even slightly larger this year. But, even though it has more surface area, the iPhone 18 Pro isn't more stable than last year's model, coming in at 66% in the 3DMark Steel Nomad Light stress test. That's just a bit worse than the 17 Pro Max, which got 69% in the same test last year, but with how much faster the A20 Pro is, I'll take it.

Apple also included a bigger battery this year, with 5,567mAh of capacity, compared to 5,088mAh in the iPhone 17 Pro Max. Apple claims that this battery will last through 30 hours of regular use, and while I don’t have a reliable way to benchmark battery life, I believe Apple’s numbers.

I have been pushing this phone for around three weeks now, and I usually only put it on the charger every other day, and the phone hasn’t died on me yet. Obviously, if you’re taking a lot of photos or playing a heavy game like Where Winds Meet, that number will go down, but even then I don’t imagine the phone dying in the course of a day.

items.title: Ali G: Who Iz I? Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
is on Prime Video now, and maybe in a theater near you, though probably not for much longer.

Once the genesis of Sacha Baron Cohen’s mockumentary career, white poseur Ali G now marks its whimper of an ending. Released on Prime Video just five days after its theatrical release, the actor’s directorial debut Ali G: Who Iz I? barely holds together as either cinema or practical joke — let alone where the two have met in the past, by way of his exceptionally enduring Borat. His efforts this time feel especially feeble, landing somewhere in the realm of an unfocused documentary, where the result isn’t so much laughter, or even provocation, but puzzled annoyance. Fifteen minutes in, one of his unsuspecting targets sums it up succinctly when shown a presentation meant to offend her: “I don’t care.”

Cohen’s latest borrows characters from both HBO’s Da Ali G show as well as his Showtime series Who Is America? in an attempt to weave a political portrait of the modern United States, all wrapped in a flimsy narrative. Like the riotous Borat sequel, Who Iz I? is nominally about the wannabe British Rastafari facing fatherhood, when he learns that his longtime girlfriend Julie (Morgana Robinson, taking over for Kellie Bright from the narrative comedy Ali G Indahouse) is pregnant with their child. An attempt to get a third season of his HBO interview series off the ground finds him flying across the pond to LA, where his arrival catches the attention of another Cohen character, Showtime’s Dr. Nira Cain-N'Degeocello, an outdated send-up of liberal academia who hopes to nail him for “cultural appropriation,” despite speaking over people himself.

Along the way, both characters interact with various bystanders in Cohen’s signature prankish style, but his instigations prove limp. There just doesn’t seem to be enough footage to string together a film of everyday subjects responding with outrage, indignation, or even the strained politeness underlying the original Borat from 2006. Two decades later, everyone seems bored by this commonplace, microcelebrity tomfoolery, whether or not they recognize the man behind the makeup. They mostly don’t, though at least one of them, involved in the movie’s confoundingly scattered climax,appears to have gone along with it for the daily rate. Perhaps this is why Cohen feels the need for heavy-handed explanations, in the movie’s opening closing, of how his mockumentary format works.

The caricatures Cohen portrays feel tame in comparison to a world increasingly divided by political fissures, though given how much the movie’s first half is concerned with “cancel culture” and “DEI” — things even the U.S. government uses as phantom boogeyman — the movie’s mission statement is too askew to root for in the first place. While it does eventually set its sights on those in power, it opts for low-hanging fruit in the form of penile humor that its subjects mostly ignore, forcing Cohen to cut awkwardly around non-reactions.

Who Iz I? is a film that takes no risks and has nothing to say, all in service of misguided self-preservation.

However, setting aside the movie’s asymmetrical political bent doesn’t yield much of interest to begin with, because Who Iz I? is really only about America on the surface. What it’s really about is Cohen, or rather Ali G, in a way that threatens to be interesting for the briefest moment. Will the character wrestle with his own irrelevance when he fails to secure airtime? Not so fast! Instead, the hamstrung plot grows increasingly obsessed with Dr. Nira’s attempts to find dirt on Ali on make him persona non grata, as though wayward online criticisms of Cohen’s shtick had gotten under his skin and he were trying to pre-empt objections to the movie through Cohen-on-Cohen discourse. If anyone was trying to silence Cohen’s comedy, they’ve clearly been unsuccessful, since he managed to make this movie — though its failures are a product of its own inability to strike while the iron is hot. A three second Cameo from isn’t going to cut it in 2026.

This is largely in line with the film’s M.O. Few gags or targets stick around long enough to let the absurdities land. The Ali G character isn’t so much deployed to prod at people’s politics as he is to be a clownish presence waving his arms for attention, while Cohen also portrays an exaggerated mishmash of what he pictures his critics are like, or what they believe. At the very least, this yields a revealing portrait of artistic insecurity, if an unintentional one. Who Iz I? is a film that takes no risks and has nothing to say, all in service of misguided self-preservation, as Cohen fails to read the tea leaves of a culture that has, for better or worse, long left him behind.

items.title: Dexter: Resurrection Season 2 Premiere Review
items.author: Matt Fowler
items.content:
This is a non-spoiler review for the Season 2 premiere, "Risky Business," which airs on Paramount+ with the Premium Plan on Friday, October 30.

Uh oh, Dexter's got that itch again. The itch to kill? Nah, that never went away. I'm talking about the more frustrating itch. The midlife crisis urge to be reckless.

In the first episode of Dexter: Resurrection's second season — which I really wish had just been given a whole new subtitle — the Bay Harbor Butcher (Michael C. Hall) is feeling a little under-appreciated for what he believes are his life-saving endeavors, and he might be looking for a spotlight of gratitude (think of the parade he imagined for himself at the end of the very first season). "Risky Business" makes for a good start to this new batch of episodes, introducing both an ansty protagonist and a few new Big Bads to contend with. Of course, one episode only gives us a small glimpse into the upcoming season and it's not enough to fully judge what's ahead, but if Dexter's "I'm over 50 now" inner turmoil and restlessness are treated differently than his past bouts of self-reflection and unease, Season 2 could be a very interesting take.

To quickly recap the journey of the series: Seasons 1 through 4 of the original show were groundbreaking. Seasons 5 through 8 were uneven, and at their worst had really bad creative turns. Dexter: New Blood was good and landed very well as a revised ending for the saga. Resurrection, while initially eliciting eye rolls because of the titular resurrection, wound up being a true return to form for the series, feeling the most like the early seasons of the first show.

One thing that remains true though, Dexter-wise, is that the story stumbles when Dexter doesn't learn from his mistakes. Sure, he's flawed and driven by a mad desire to spill blood. He stretches himself too thin and will also kill an innocent person in a pinch in order to escape capture. There's also a self-destructive element to him that we accept. It's enticing. What we don't want is him to be a bonehead who resets anew every season. So far, in the wake of "Risky Business," we're safe. After dealing with Peter Dinklage's Leon Prater and his gruesome gallery of both murderous memorabilia and actual maniacs in Resurrection Season 1, Dex has realized that he's a big deal. Too big to be toiling away as a ride share driver, for sure, and maybe even too big to let poor James Doakes (Erik King) go down as the Butcher. Perhaps things need to get a bit more... public.

'Risky Business' makes for a good start to this new batch of episodes, introducing both an ansty protagonist and a few new Big Bads to contend with.

While Dexter is busy feeling time's encroaching talons, we catch up with Harrison (Jack Alcott), keeping the Morgan family cop tradition alive as an NYPD rookie. How will Harrison deal with his dad pushing things to the edge? Ultimately, where will his loyalties lie, once again, if push comes to shove and Dexter starts kicking up dirt? Because there's darkness on the horizon. Not only is wise Detective Wallace (Kadia Saraf) still around, and taking notice of Harrison's new career, but madmen like the New York Ripper (Wallace's white whale from last season) and the hot-off-the-presses Five Borough Killer are making things super slicey and dicey out there. Fun casting alert for those two, by the way, with "first-ever on-screen Hannibal Lecter" Brian Cox as the Ripper and a stoic, menacing Dan Stevens as FBK.

The juice of "Risky Business" involves Dexter tying up Prater's loose ends, which means Eric Stonestreet's Al Walker returns to get some more time in the sun. Here, Stonestreet shows a much more dangerous, horrifying side to his Rapunzel killer, playing even more against his Modern Family persona. I won't go into any more guest star/adversary/obstacle details than what I've already divulged, but "Risky Business" plays well, sets the table nicely, and even has some inspired '80s punk rock needle drops.

items.title: Marvel's VisionQuest Episodes 5 & 6 Recap and Review
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Episodes 5 & 6, which are streaming now on Disney+.

At this point, I'm fully on board with VisionQuest and the story of robotic reinvention it's telling. But as compelling as Paul Bettany's White Vision is, he's small potatoes compared to the series' real star, James Spader's Ultron. Episodes 5 and 6 go all-in with Ultron and his romantic obsession with the fair robo-lady Jocasta (T'Nia Miller), and the results are pretty darned impressive.

That's especially true of Episode 5, which is definitely the high point for VisionQuest so far. This one kinda, sorta takes the form of a bottle episode, as Vision and his fellow A.I. units find themselves locked in Ultron's attic prison and forced to observe his machinations from afar. This episode is cleverly constructed in how it presents bits and pieces of Ultron's conversations from different vantage points while still leaving the character's true motivations somewhat shrouded in mystery. As ever, the series gets a lot of mileage out of conveying complex digital processes through very hokey, analog representations. See also - the exorcism scene from Episode 4.

Visually, Episode 5 is a real treat. I really enjoyed the transitions between grainy video footage and more elaborately staged black-and-white environments. There's a very cozy feel to Ultron's conversations with Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) and Jocasta that serves to highlight the dialogue and the tense back-and-forth. Having Vision and his full-color comrades patrolling in the background only makes the whole effect work that much better. It's almost like watching a well-choreographed stage play unfold.

Ultimately, though, it all comes down to the terrific chemistry between Spader and Miller. Sure, the earlier Tommy/Ultron conversation is strong, but even that can't hold a candle to the pure scenery-chewing fun of watching Ultron and Jocasta take each other's measure. Miller is able to bring a whole new level of nuance and charm to her role in this more human form, and she expertly matches Spader's gravelly blend of menance and good humor. I almost didn't want their exchange to end, but at least that element carries over into Episode 6.

Both the Ultron/Tommy and Ultron/Jocasta scenes do a fantastic job of exploring the troubled psychology of this maladjusted creation of Tony Stark and Bruce Banner. Tommy cuts right to the heart of the matter when he accuses Ultron of failing to understand connection. Yet paired with Jocasta, Ultron feels the pull anyway. He was already a fascinating villain in his original cinematic appearance, but the series has found newer and more complex layers to delve into. And now, though his intentions are entirely self-serving, he's no longer so clear-cut an antagonist.

Given how enthralling Episode 5 is, it should come as no surprise that Episode 6 is a bit of a comedown in comparison. After a bottle episode spent in purely digital space, it's a slight adjustment getting used to a more real-world conflict and the return of Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Part of me would be just as happy to see that character shuffled offstage, but Episode 6 does eventually justify his return. There's a fun little standoff between Vision and Paladin that unexpectedly leads to the two enemies becoming temporary allies, and the reveal that the Handler (Diane Morgan) is herself an oppressed AI unit is an amusing twist (as is the MCU origin of Tommy's Speed codename).

Both the Ultron/Tommy and Ultron/Jocasta scenes do a fantastic job of exploring the troubled psychology of this maladjusted creation of Tony Stark and Bruce Banner.

What this episode doesn't quite justify, however, is the sudden and inexplicable return of Faran Tahir's Raza. On some level, it's sort of neat seeing the very first MCU bad guy putting in an appearance nearly 20 years later, but why dust off that old chestnut in an Iron Man-free context? The character doesn't serve any particular purpose beyond providing Vision and Paladin with the necessary goons to battle, and he's taken out of the picture as suddenly as he appears. It comes across as continuity mining for the sake of continuity mining.

Fortunately, Episode 6 does still have a healthy dose of Ultron/Jocasta banter to fall back upon, and that's where the series continues to shine brightest. The interplay between the two characters really is the show's biggest selling point now. Every time it seems we've sussed out Ultron's motivations or that the character has bitten off more than he can chew with Jocasta, he surprises us again. We still don't know who the ultimate villain of the series is meant to be (Phineas Horton? J.I.M.?), but I'm having a blast on the road to VisionQuest's endgame.

items.title: Lupin: Part 4 Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
It’s been three years since Lupin’s — a less memorable, less focused entry — so you’d be forgiven for forgetting much of what transpired. The show’s fourth part features an extended recap narrated by the title character before kicking off in earnest, at which point it hits the “soft reboot” button, both narratively and stylistically. Its biggest change is a welcome one: it leans unapologetically into the soap opera underpinnings which have always made it tick. The result is a brisk eight episodes that, despite wheel-spinning near the season’s end, eventually find their way to the kind of ludicrous melodrama that makes the French heist series such a turn-your-brain-off delight.

Part 3 ended with a major cliffhanger, as gentleman thief Assane Diop (Omar Sy) — a devotee of Maurice Leblanc’s fictitious fraudster Arsène Lupin — found himself in prison, in a cell adjacent to his long time, opulent enemy Hubert Pellegrini (Hervé Pierre). How does the new season resolve this tension? Well, it doesn’t. Which is to say, it treats the whole thing like a gag in order for the show to move forward into unexpected territory. Four years have passed, and in that time, Assane has willingly remained behind bars — except for a brief escape where he bamboozled Pellegrini all the way into a shipping container bound for a Malaysian prison. Now on the verge of release for good behavior, it finally seems like Assane has turned over a new leaf. That is, until a slickly-executed pair of simultaneous heists, in his signature style, make the police suspicious, forcing him to go rogue in order to prove his innocence.

During Assane’s prison stint, his teenage son Raoul (now played by newcomer Théo Christine) has grown into a frustrated young adult in want of an absent father. Once a mere plot device and kidnapping victim, Raoul now becomes the series’ unexpected heart and soul, though the narrative, and Assane, keep shoving him to the side until those frustrations reach a boiling point. A winding conspiracy takes precedence, involving a copycat swindler and twists and turns ripped right from a daytime soap opera — a secret lineage, sudden deaths, equally sudden resurrections, and so on — forcing Lupin to unexpectedly turn to former foes for new partnerships in search of a secret treasure. All the while, his police frenemy Youssef Guédira (Soufiane Guerrab), a fellow Leblanc enthusiast, remains on his tail, but is less willing to offer him the benefit of doubt when his partner Sofia Belkacem (Shirine Boutella) is gravely injured.

It's a brisk eight episodes that, despite wheel-spinning near season’s end, eventually find their way to the kind of ludicrous melodrama that makes the series such a turn-your-brain-off delight.

Complicating matters further is the fact that, in Assane’s absence, his best friend and co-conman Benjamin (Antoine Gouy) has fallen for his ex-wife and Raoul’s mother, Claire (Ludivine Sagnier), adding yet another layer to the sprawling flashbacks of the various characters as teens and young adults. Was this pairing always in the cards? Of course not, but the fourth season also goes a long way towards re-writing the show’s basic DNA. These flashbacks involve both interpersonal drama and a surprising amount of setup for the contemporary conspiracies, as though the central plot of this season — involving a secret society with some icky blood-purity leanings, playing into the show’s modern, pluralistic re-imagining of Leblanc’s Lupin — had been decades in the making. Like Assane himself, the show is a bullshit artist of the highest caliber; it works to convince you that every twisting screw is part of some intricately devised puzzle dating back to its 2021 debut, when it’s all clearly been designed on-the-fly.

And yet, that design yields some clockwork thrills from time to time, between Assane’s continued weaponization of racial prejudice to pull off his galaxy-brained heists (one scheme in particular involves a flashmob of re-enactors dressed as an oft-forgotten Black French general) and the style with which the series presents each deceit. The editing is more judicious this time. To reveal how a given ploy was pulled off, it relies less on unseen angles and elements when episodes re-visit existing scenes, and more on parts of the image you might’ve missed in the first place.

The season’s broader themes of family allow Lupin to become a particularly silly bit of business akin to the later Fast & Furious films. Assane becomes increasingly torn between making up for lost time with Raoul and tracking down lost jewels with a newly-formed family of thieves who start out the season at odds. Among these is a mixed-race character named Adèle Kapoor (Laïka Blanc-Francard) who, in addition to expanding the show’s quickfire (if malformed) invocations of racism in modern France, becomes the center of a tech-infused update to the series with her skills as a hacker in the age of A.I. deepfakes. The less said about her backstory beforehand, the better, but that she’s on par with Assane as a Leblanc-inspired burglar and gives him a much-needed rival and dramatic counterweight.

The show’s new directions aren’t necessarily original — here you’ll find familiar gadgets, scenes and dynamics straight out of everything from Bond, Indiana Jones and Mission: Impossible to the network procedural White Collar — but Lupin’s fourth part sublimates all these influences into something cheekily enjoyable. It rides a fine line between heightened, crisscrossing nonsense plots and intensified character-centric schmaltz, but when it counts the most, it manages to find just the right balance between the two, before leaving off in perhaps the most unexpected place this series could go. If there is a fifth season (and there really should be), the dilemmas facing Assane will probably make for damn good television, given the various pieces Part 4 moves gradually into place.

items.title: The Wolf Among Us Remastered Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
With intense performances, a heady atmosphere, and sharp writing, The Wolf Among Us’ gripping neo-noir saga rivalled the prestige TV dramas of the time when it first came out in 2013, earning acclaim as one of Telltale’s greatest yet. Now, with a long-awaited sequel in the works, it’s been given a fresh coat of paint that’s gussied up locations and added a slew of behind-the-scenes content to sweeten the pot. Some holdover annoyances haven’t been addressed, like the original’s stiff and occasionally uncanny animations, which get in the way of The Wolf Among Us Remastered feeling truly definitive. Still, this story remains a fantastic one, and the enhanced set dressing even manages to deepen its sinister mood.

For those who didn’t play the original, The Wolf Among Us thoughtfully adapts Bill Willingham’s beloved graphic novel series Fables, in which folklore characters covertly coexist with humans in a New York suburb aptly called Fabletown. Set roughly 20 years earlier as a non-canon prequel, Telltale’s adaptation artfully draws on classic noir storytelling, dropping you into the shoes of Sheriff Bigby (aka the Big Bad Wolf) to solve a bizarre but gripping murder. With a decapitated head on his stoop and little more to go on than a ribbon and an etched ring, the marshal must use his keen nose and perception to find the culprit… and he has to do it fast. With humans investigating the case and the social fabric of the mythical community at stake, failure could cause their secret society to collapse entirely.

On top of that already immense pressure, there’s one more important piece of subtext to consider: after centuries of violence as a storybook baddie, Bigby’s constituents don’t necessarily trust him to get the job done and, naturally, watch his every move. As such, he’s forced to lean on familiar faces like Snow White, The Little Mermaid, and Bufkin from The Wizard of Oz to chase leads as he unravels a web of complex issues spanning class consciousness, poverty, and abuses of power. It’s a journey that proves to be thoroughly engrossing.

To peel back the seedy underbelly of Fabletown, your time as Bigby is loosely split into segments. For the most part, you’ll have intriguing conversations from a third-person perspective, choosing from a handful of responses as a clock quickly ticks down. Through this system, you can lean on witnesses who seem to be hiding something, threatening them if they continue to hold back. Or, if all else fails, you can resort to physical violence (assuming that aligns with your own moral compass). Cleverly, the language used in these interactions draws on its fairy tale source material without ever feeling corny. So, despite including terms like Witching Well and Magic Mirror, the conversations remain emotionally charged – a tribute to the writing underneath and the resonant, enduring performances of its cast.

Conversations cleverly draw on the fairy tale source material without ever feeling corny.

What’s most important is that your reactions here are not one-sided. As you make certain decisions, a threatening notification pops up stating that the character you’re interacting with will remember what you did (a staple of the genre). For example, say you make a promise to deliver something and don’t come through – well, they might have a few choice words for you the next time you meet. In this way, The Wolf Among Us is not just about solving the whodunit; it is also about choosing whether Bigby will shake off his villainous origins and prove his status as Sheriff and protector.

What’s neat is that the choice is mostly up to you. If you want to, you can cruelly push the citizens to get your answers, or try as often as you might to take their side, even if that means going against the legal institution to which you are professionally bound. By exploring this curious grey area, I began to understand why the residents of Fabletown act as they do, eventually allowing me to empathise with their actions, no matter how desperate or depraved they may be.

Amidst these social calls, you’ll occasionally control Bigby directly as he picks through dingy locations – such as dive bars and ornate offices – interacting with clues to advance the investigation. Just like in conversations, there are even more ethical quandaries to consider, like whether you should interrupt a wake like an unemotional jerk or kick in a door instead of knocking like a gentleman. As the confusing haze of right and wrong settled in, I frequently struggled to maintain my good-guy persona, especially when provoked. It would be so easy to smack an obvious bad guy in the head to get the answers I needed more quickly, but then wouldn’t I be just as bad as him?

Last but not least are the interactive sequences, which require you to complete a series of quick time events to survive some of the higher octane moments throughout the tale. You’ll rip out throats, jump across city blocks, and even set broken bones, with failure occasionally leading to a game over. Thankfully, frequent checkpoints drop you right back into the action if you miss a beat. The variety and frequency of these moments do well to keep you busy as you piece together the killer's identity, particularly as many of them arrive with mesmerising (and sometimes gruesome) animations.

Quick time events arrive with mesmerising (and sometimes gruesome) animations.

Mirroring the flow of the original, The Wolf Among Us Remastered takes place over five episodes that are about two hours long (all included in this single package instead of being sold individually). For the most part, the choices you make feel impactful, which keeps the momentum chugging along nicely. That is, until the penultimate episode, when the pace suddenly dips and characters start needlessly reiterating their points of view. In earlier episodes, I’d look under every stone to figure out who the villain was, and I was fairly confident I understood what was going on by episode four, so everything slowing down right when I was ready for the payoff felt slightly disjointed.

I do get why they didn’t alter this chapter more substantially; this is a remaster, not a remake, and major story alterations could ultimately do more harm than good if handled poorly. Besides, there are still enjoyable chats throughout the episode, so the dragging is only a minor blip in an otherwise brilliant story, with a finale that certainly clawed me back. But when the rest of the tale is so tight and considered, it’s still a bit annoying to spend a couple of hours rehashing information you’ve already worked hard to uncover.

That dissatisfaction is also softened by the fact that the locations you visit are so intentionally designed and brilliantly reflect the personalities of their inhabitants. While Bigby's tiny, sparsely furnished flat fits with his lone wolf status, the local watering hole’s scrappy yet warm atmosphere matches its down-on-their-luck clientele. The remaster's design glow-up further bolsters that environmental storytelling, as everything from couch upholstery to pawn shop artefacts has been redesigned with far more detail. For instance, those familiar with Aunt Greenleaf's apartment will see that it’s now even witchier than before, with hanging tassels and strewn curios. Elsewhere, the infamous Puddin ‘n’ Pie remains seedy but stylish, featuring Art Nouveau-esque pendant lights and extravagant neon piping.

With so much effort spent on the look, it’s a shame that not every detail received the same touch, and that there are still a handful of friction points on the technical side. Characters sometimes move as if on a swivel, and Bigby’s animations when finding clues tend to feel strangely rigid and occasionally robotic. In the 2013 original, these blips were passable, but in a 2026 remaster, the awkward animations and jerky movements stand out. That’s not to say they are so distracting that they undo all the impressive polishing elsewhere, just that I wish those edges had been similarly smoothed over in order to soundly mark this as the definitive version of the tale.

Harkening back to a simpler era of DVD extras, The Wolf Among Us Remastered also includes a gaggle of bonus features for fans who might want a peek behind the curtain of development. There’s a toggleable Noir game mode that lets you play out the tale in black and white, a digital gallery that compares old art stills with new ones, plus developer and cast interviews about the making-of. As someone who likes to sift through every scrap of lore, I found these additions certainly fun to pilfer through… even if the interface is a tad old-fashioned, leaning more toward sentiment than usefulness. The most compelling add by far is a handful of playable deleted scenes that, while rough around the edges, highlight interesting plot threads and deviations that are exciting to experience after the final credits roll.

items.title: We Build Star Wars Executor Super Star Destroyer, the Longest Build in LEGO History
items.author: Chris Reed
items.content:
It might be that the designers are bumping against the upper limit of how long a set can be while also remaining commercially viable. Since I built the Executor, it's been sitting on the work desk in my house, and nothing else can fit on that desk at the same time. The first thing you'll want to do, before you even think of buying this set, is make sure you have the room to display it. It is 7.5 inches high, 53.5 inches long, and 20 inches wide. To illustrate how big that is more subjectively: I could easily believe this build was a show display – the type of thing you might see at a LEGO convention or in a toy museum, under glass – rather than a set available for retail purchase, as this one is.

The LEGO Executor Super Star Destroyer comes in two separate boxes, spread out over 54 bags and four instruction booklets. The first thing you build is a tiny Imperial Star Destroyer Devastator. This is one of the first ships we see in Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope when it's chasing after the Tantive IV, during the scene where Leia escapes with the Death Star plans.

I actually built a 4,784-piece LEGO model of the Devastator back in 2019, which came with a tiny model of the Tantive IV to highlight its disparate size. So when this new set shows how the Executor dwarfs even the Devastator, and makes it look miniscule by comparison? It illustrates the massive scale these ships possess.

After building the micro-Devastator, you build a minifigure-scaled bridge of the Executor. It's famous for being the location in Star Wars Episode V: The Empire Strikes Back, where Darth Vader speaks to six bounty hunters – Boba Fett, Bossk, IG-88, 4-LOM, Zuckuss, and Dengar – and offers a bounty for the capture of the Millennium Falcon. He infamously fixes Fett with an intimidating stare: "I want them alive. NO DISINTEGRATIONS."

This is the first time all six bounty hunters have been packaged in the same set. LEGO is more likely to be completionist with its giant sets (like or ). It doesn't justify the high prices, admittedly. But it's still nice that LEGO treats its prestige sets like standalone purchases rather than parts of a "collect 'em all' money scheme.

Next, you build the black stand. It is surprisingly durable; it will later be the only stable means by which you can move the model from one location to another. During the build itself, you use the black stand to turn the model upside down, to better access and construct the underbelly of the ship.

Finally, you begin building the Executor itself, starting with its foundational framework. But unlike other LEGO frameworks, which are expansive and airy to create the illusion of bulk, the LEGO Executor has a lean, compact build. A dense mass of multicolored Technic parts forms the model's triangular silhouette.

The work goes slowly and meticulously. This is not a build you can speed through, and it is very easy to miss a step or forget to insert this eye into that rod, which will cause the final build to fall apart, literally. I had to backtrack a few times to make sure it all fit properly, knowing the stability of one element relied upon the underlying stability of another.

Anytime there's an open hook or clamp, it means one of two things. Either you forgot to connect an element from the last bag, or there's another element, which you'll build several hours from now, that fits into it perfectly. As massive as it is, this set doesn't have any stray bits for the hell of it. Every brick is functional.

The build repeats at times, but it doesn't feel laborious. You'll build one layering plate, and you'll build its mirror counterpart an hour later. By that time, you've forgotten the process and it feels new again.

One important caution: Have steady hands, and do not, under any circumstances, drop a piece into the build itself. There's nothing more painful than trying to fish out an errant brick, while you hear it rattling about. In the process of getting one piece, another piece falls off, or a structure collapses into itself. If you try and repair that, another piece falls off or a different structure collapses.

I speak from experience. I made one mistake, and in the process of undoing it, it cost me an hour to rebuild what I had broken. And at the end of it – after putting everything back to where it should have been – I still had four pieces left over, and I couldn't figure where they went. I hope they're not too important, because I'm not digging under the hood again to figure them out.

This model's size is one thing, but its level of detail, painstakingly integrated into the build's top side, is quite another. Star Wars creator George Lucas called it "greebles"—the application of disparate mechanical parts to an otherwise smooth surface to give it texture. Because the ship is gray and because the "greebling" overlaying it is also gray, it appears, from a distance, like a monochromatic monolith.

But move closer, and you gain an appreciation for its scale. Where did the crew members live and spend their leisure time? Where did they man the guns? Where did they navigate and initiate the thrusters? Did they commute from one end of the ship to the other, or did they simply inhabit one part of the ship for their entire service, never seeing the whole?

According to canon, the Executor was larger than Manhattan, and over 280,000 crew members worked and died on it. The width of several tiles represents the length of several city blocks. A single piece of greebling represents a machine bigger than a building. This is a floating city in the sky, and to build it is to feel and appreciate its weight. And after you've finished it? The build's size and complexity render it contemplative. It somehow gets more interesting and engrossing, the more you look at it.

LEGO Star Wars: Executor Super Star Destroyer, Set #75457, retails for $799.99, and it is composed of 6130 pieces. It is available for purchase now at

items.title: The Simpsons: 'Treehouse of Horror XXXVII' Review
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
: "Treehouse of Horror XXXVII."

While it's best to go into modern "Treehouse of Horror" episodes with tempered expectations, the truth is that The Simpsons' track record with Halloween specials has improved a fair bit in recent years. "Treehouse of Horror XXXVII" is far from the strongest the series has ever delivered, but nor is it anywhere near the weakest. Its main flaw is in being a just plain decent episode in the immediate aftermath of the much superior "Treehouse of Horror Presents: The Revengening."

Unlike last week's special, which focused on one singular storyline involving Homer (Dan Castellaneta) and his compatriots being hounded by a bloodthirsty slasher villain with a surprising secret identity, this episode reverts to the traditional "Treehouse" formula. That means a cleverly animated intro sequence (in this case, a neat little claymation parody of The Nightmare Before Christmas) followed by three spooky shorts. My main takeaway from watching these two episodes back-to-back is that the series really ought to consider switching to the full-length episode format more permanently. But if the plan is to start doing both every year, then who are we to complain, really?

If there's no one particular standout segment in this year's "Treehouse," at least there aren't any weak links, either. The episode opens with the cleverly titled "Bride's Shed Revisited," as Marge (Julie Kavner) assembles a backyard shed that winds up switching out husbands at random. It's amusing to watch Marge lean into her dubious new power and cycle through the best and worst eligible mates Springfield has to offer, culminating in Survivor host Jeff Probst. I can even forgive the idea of Marge hooking up with Probst, since this episode is (as Lisa reminds us in the intro) strictly non-canon.

That's followed by "Dog Boy Afternoon," a very loose Pet Sematary parody that sees Homer accidentally kill both Santa's Little Helper and Bart (Nancy Cartwright) and inadvertantly cause their corpses to switch brains. It's a fun little segment that benefits both from the recurring gag of Homer drinking his way through morning and afternoon-themed liquor and the general body-swap comedy. There's also a surprising amount of gore here, particularly in the scene where Homer is ripped apart by hungry dogs. It's always nice to see these Halloween specials push the envelope in that regard.

Finally, there's "Vehicular Dad Slaughter," as teen versions of Bart and Lisa (Yeardley Smith) discover their dear old dad has been imprisoned in DMV training video limbo by Patty and Selma (Kavner). I like that writer Tim Long opted to jump forward in time for this segment, even if the segment could just as easily have been executed with the traditional characters. Patty and Selma also make for solid witchy antagonists here.

If there are any unifying themes to this year's special, it's the emphasis on exploring the Simpsons clan at different eras of their lives and in spotlighting Kavner's characters over the rest of the ensemble cast. Both work to the episode's benefit. The focus on Marge and her sisters might have given me pause in seasons past, as Kavner's voice has deteriorated quite a bit over the years (granted, the same could be said for several cast members of this nearly 40-year-old sitcom). But whether through some sort of digital AI assistance or just plain effort on her part, that's another area the series has improved upon of late. Kavner's Marge sounds closer to her old self these days.

Again, none of these three segments are good enough to rival the all-time "Treehouse of Horror" classics, but nor are there any stinkers this time. That's still only enough to make "Treehouse of Horror XXXVII" the second-best Halloween episode of Season 38.

items.title: Phantom Blade Zero Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Phantom Blade Zero has spent years looking almost too good to be true, especially coming from a studio that's best known for its mobile games. That’s why it's just about the biggest compliment I can pay it that after 50 hours performing picture-perfect kung fu, it's exactly as fun to play as it looks. This effortlessly smooth action game has some of the most satisfying and well-tuned combat I’ve played in a long time, a surprising number of secrets to discover and quests to complete in each of its beautiful levels, and a neverending supply of clever encounters full of unbelievably awesome moments. Its convoluted story and occasional performance issues may not live up to that incredible action, but it nails just about everything else, and there were only a handful of moments where I wasn’t absolutely thrilled to be slicing my way through the ranks of the Wulin.

Phantom Blade Zero plays like something straight out of a wuxia epic. As a metal-as-hell martial artist of mysterious origins with only 66 days left alive to exact your revenge, you set out on an odyssey across the ruined lands of the Phantom World, facing off against all manner of beast and badass along the way. The story here isn’t Phantom Blade Zero’s strong suit as it tries to do a bit too much, shoving in a whole bunch of mystical jargon, dozens of characters, and a needlessly complex timeline, very little of which ultimately pays off anyway. In the first couple hours alone, so much time is spent toggling back and forth between present day, several years ago, several months ago, and several days ago that I was exhausted by all the exposition before I’d even faced my first real boss fight. That said, there are enough likeable characters along the way, especially your unflappable hero named Soul, that I was usually able to forgive it for occasionally wasting my time with unnecessary flashbacks and lengthy explanations.

Besides, you’ll be spending most of your time exploring the world and squaring off against enemies big and small, and it’s pretty clear that Phantom Blade Zero wants you to spend most of your attention on this part of the adventure. And that’s a good thing, too, because by God is it good. It only took a couple minutes for the precise parry and dodge mechanics to feel natural, and the nuanced but not-overly-complex system of weapons, combos, special abilities, and upgrades are rolled out at an extremely smart pace, all of which are easy enough to slip into like a tailored set of flowing wuxia robes. I’m a complete snob when it comes to the feel and pacing of combat in these types of games, so the fact that this immediately felt like reuniting with an old friend made it instantly compelling, and it’s one of those intangible things that’s very hard to get right.

Even more impressive is that not only does the combat feel good right away, it does so across dozens of weapons, each with their own unique moveset. This game that doesn’t just encourage you to change up your weapon loadout at regular intervals, it actually requires you to mix things up since swapping your active melee weapon is one of the ways you can restore your posture meter with a single button press. And since many enemies, particularly bosses, can instantly drain your posture with certain attacks, you’ll be swapping between different options with regularity, forcing you to commit multiple movesets and special abilities to memory. Conveniently, Phantom Blade Zero makes it extremely easy for you to reclaim and reallocate points invested in leveling up weapons, so there’s rarely any reason to stick with a set loadout anyway – especially since you always seem to find the exact tool you need right before entering an area or encountering a boss where it would come in handy. For example, I noticed that I found a water cannon weapon only a few feet away from an area that led to a fire-based boss. Nice.

Combat feels good right away, even across dozens of unique weapons.

Beyond that, you’ll unlock a bunch of additional tools like grappling hooks and bows, which have utility both in combat encounters and outside of them since you can use them to reach certain parts of the map or break through barriers that are otherwise impassable. There are also trinkets that offer interesting buffs, like a significant damage increase when you’re at full health, and a skill tree with perks that let you do things like execute a dodge while in mid-air or increase the number of healing items you can carry. There’s a surprising amount of depth to the things you can upgrade and the ways to customize exactly how your Wulin warrior does his thing, and I spent much more time than I typically do in these kinds of games just testing out different weapons and swapping my equipment around as a result. At the very least, it’s worth doing so just to see the unique execution animations when you finish off trash enemies.

You’ll have plenty of time to try them all out as you get your steps in across Phantom Blade Zero’s eight maps, too. Each one is filled with foes to take down, side quests to complete, chests to loot, and secrets to discover. A surprising amount of the places to go and people to meet are completely missable, including the entirety of a very cool questline that sees you getting trained by none other than Donnie Yen as the mysterious gold-masked man (which is actually one of PBZ’s strongest subplots). While most of the side quests are pretty straightforward missions to go somewhere and collect some stuff for a small reward, they gave me more reasons to spend time exploring every nook and cranny, which I was happy to do. And unlike lots of modern games filled with icons on the screen telling you exactly where to go and what to do, Phantom Blade Zero instead makes use of hand-drawn maps that only give you a vague idea of your location in relation to key landmarks, allowing you to explore and fill in the gaps on your own.

If there’s one thing that consistently mucks up this journey, it’s that Phantom Blade Zero suffers from some pretty bad geometry. Soul gets caught on surfaces all the time, and even the tiniest bumps in the road can stop him dead in his tracks, which is pretty hilarious for a guy who can jump 40 feet in the air while doing 19 backflips. Not only that, there are invisible borders all over the place that make exploration janky at times, especially when platforming sections ask you to get to a specific ledge, only for you to discover there’s an invisible wall and you fall to your death. I died nearly 200 times over the course of my playthrough, and roughly half of those deaths were me falling into a pit or getting caught in the environment until I was able to get myself killed or reload my save file. In one case, I even lost about 20 minutes of progress when my supposed martial master couldn’t escape from some bushes. Oh, and enemies occasionally get stuck in the environment too, which just makes fights where it happens feel so lame.

Despite that, Phantom Blade Zero’s superpower – the magic trick it performs time and time again – is its way of making you feel like you’re the only person in the world badass enough to withstand its utterly insane flurry of swords against godlike monsters like it’s nothing. The truth is that the melee dance of combat encounters is just so finely tuned, with every attack telegraphed just enough to give you exactly the time you need to react, aided by an almost imperceptible musical rhythm that grants you a certain level of precognition for what’s going to happen next. Once I synced up with its tempo, I started anticipating attacks before I consciously registered them, leading me to perfectly block some lightning-quick attack I hadn’t seen before. There’s nothing specifically special about my reaction time or skill with action games – rather it's a testament to how incredibly well-balanced and smartly designed these unbelievably sick fights are. It’s without question the thing Phantom Blade Zero does best, and it’s an illusion I fell for repeatedly, from the opening sequence all the way to the final battle.

I played on the hardest difficulty, and the tuning consistently felt exactly right.

Something I admire about Phantom Blade Zero’s difficulty is how consistently it feels exactly right – not too unforgiving, but it rarely lets you feel like you aren’t in danger of getting your butt kicked. I’m typically someone who relishes a challenge from games like this and so played Phantom Blade Zero on its hardest difficulty exclusively, but found myself beating just about every major boss fight in two or three tries, plus a good chunk that I cleared in one go – and I didn’t mind that one bit! It meant that I rarely saw enough of a boss to know every tool in their murder belt, and refreshingly made me feel like the one to be feared rather than the other way around. It’s pretty damn cool to enter a room and watch a 10-foot-tall badass with an eight-pack swing around a blade and think, “oh, man. This guy’s totally screwed.”

Part of the way this Goldilocks level of difficulty is achieved is due to the interesting decision to not make you repeat phases of a boss fight that you’ve already cleared. If you get through a first phase that just makes the bad guy mad and then get killed after he turns into an even more hulked-out psycho, you’ll pick back up at the top of that second phase. I’ve been known to get annoyed at having to replay the first phase of a boss fight a dozen times just to get another run at the more challenging part, to the point where multi-phase boss fights in general can get on my nerves these days. By removing this annoyance entirely, it got rid of a lot of potential friction with some of these encounters

It also allows for more freedom in how these encounters are designed, like moments where a boss uses a cheap move that one-shots you instantly if you get hit by it. Normally, including insta-kill moves like that is a good way to send me into a rage, but because my progress was almost never set back far enough to bother getting mad about, I felt a lot more lenient toward that kind of thing. I mean, let’s face it, that crazy attack where you get impaled on a giant spear, then set on fire and smashed face-first into the floor probably kill you right away, so it’s pretty neat that Phantom Blade Zero found a way to make a devastating moment like that exciting rather than irritating.

It’s also incredibly impressive that throughout the 50 hours it took me to reach credits, as I fought dozens and dozens of bosses, I was continually surprised by the creative enemies it threw at me. Sure, there’s the occasional big-guy-with-a-big-axe or dude-with-sword-you-swear-you-fought-already, but these are by far the exception, not the rule. At one point I found myself wearing a lion dancer mask, jumping around on poles to collect heads of lettuce to power up my fire blast, and in another section I fought a posse of warriors who worked together as one unit to throw preposterously intricate attacks my way – the main threat to my life there was getting caught with my guard down because I was too busy cackling. The boss fights are so consistently interesting, memorable, and numerous that I felt utterly compelled to seek out each and every one of them, which led me to turn this first playthrough into a full-on completionist run to avoid FOMO.

When I previewed Phantom Blade Zero a little over a month ago, one of my primary concerns was how it would perform, and thankfully the version I played for this review had a far more consistent performance. The framerate was much steadier, with only a few times I can recall ever noticing issues during combat. That said, there’s one map in particular where the framerate was consistently pretty terrible, specifically on a part of the map where something seems to not be working right. This feels like the type of thing that could pretty easily be identified and fixed, so I’d be surprised if a patch doesn’t arrive at or shortly after launch, but it’s worth shouting out since I suspect there are other lingering issues hiding about.
